title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 39
text:
F3 — Enterprise Architecture & Technology 
Design
Foundation
Purpose
Build your ability to understand how business strategy, capabilities, information, applications, 
technology, security, and operating models fit together — and how an IT leader makes sound 
architectural decisions without needing to be the deepest technical specialist.
Architecture is not drawing diagrams. It is the discipline of making technology choices that serve the 
enterprise over time. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to look at an enterprise technology 
landscape and answer:
"Does this technology architecture enable the business strategy — or is the organisation simply 
accumulating technology?"
That is the key distinction North Star seeks to preserve.
F3.1 — What Is Enterprise Architecture?
Enterprise Architecture (EA) is not a department. It is not a set of diagrams. It is not a compliance 
exercise. It is a disciplined way of thinking about how technology serves the enterprise — and a 
governance mechanism for ensuring that technology decisions align with strategy, integrate 
coherently, and sustain value over time.
This distinction matters. Many organisations have an "architecture team" that produces artifacts no one 
reads, reviews projects after decisions are already made, or enforces standards that stifle innovation. 
That is not architecture. That is bureaucracy wearing architecture's clothes.
What Enterprise Architecture really means is this: a continuous practice of understanding the 
current state of the enterprise's technology, envisioning a target state that serves future strategy, and 
defining the path between them — while making disciplined decisions about what to build, what to buy, 
what to integrate, what to retire, and what to tolerate.
Why EA exists is simple. Without it, technology grows organically — project by project, vendor by 
vendor, decision by decision — until the enterprise is entangled in a web of redundant systems, brittle 
integrations, escalating costs, and hidden risks. Architecture is the counterforce to entropy. It is the 
discipline that ensures technology serves the enterprise, not the other way around.
39

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 40
text:
EA vs. Solution Architecture vs. Technical Architecture are three levels of the same discipline:

Enterprise Architecture operates at the highest level. It defines the overall structure: business 
capabilities, technology domains, integration patterns, security posture, and strategic direction. It 
answers: *What should our technology ecosystem look like, and why?*

Solution Architecture operates at the initiative level. It designs how specific projects or 
programmes fit within the enterprise architecture: which systems to use, how they connect, what 
standards apply. It answers: *How do we deliver this capability within our architectural 
boundaries?*

Technical Architecture operates at the component level. It specifies the detailed design of 
individual systems: databases, APIs, infrastructure, code patterns. It answers: *How is this system 
built, and what technologies does it use?*
These levels are connected, not separate. Enterprise architecture without solution architecture is 
abstract. Solution architecture without enterprise architecture is isolated. Technical architecture 
without either is disconnected from purpose.
Architecture as a bridge between strategy and technology is its essential function. Strategy defines 
what the enterprise wants to achieve. Technology provides the means. Architecture is the disciplined 
translation between them: ensuring that technology choices serve strategic intent, that investments are 
coherent, and that the enterprise does not accumulate technical debt faster than it creates value.
Architecture principles and standards are the guardrails. Principles are enduring rules that guide 
decisions: "Buy before build unless differentiation requires custom development." "Cloud-first for new 
applications." "Security by design, not as an afterthought." Standards are the specific implementations: 
approved platforms, mandated integration patterns, required security controls. Principles provide 
direction. Standards provide consistency. Both must evolve as the enterprise and its context change.
The role of the CIO / IT Director in architecture is not to draw diagrams or select technologies 
personally. It is to ensure that architecture exists as a living discipline, that architectural decisions are 
made with appropriate rigor and speed, that the architecture function has authority and credibility, and 
that the board and executive team understand the architectural implications of their strategic choices. 
The CIO is the sponsor of architecture. The architect is its practitioner. Both are accountable for its 
effectiveness.
40

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 41
text:
F3.2 — The Enterprise Architecture Domains
Figure — Enterprise architecture domains
Architecture is not a single view. It is a set of interconnected lenses, each revealing a different 
dimension of the enterprise technology system.
The major domains are:

Business Architecture — the capabilities, processes, value streams, and organisational structures 
that define what the enterprise does

Data & Information Architecture — the data domains, flows, ownership, quality, and platforms 
that make information an enterprise asset

Application Architecture — the portfolio of systems, their relationships, their lifecycles, and their 
alignment to business capabilities

Technology Architecture — the infrastructure, platforms, networks, and compute resources that 
underpin applications and services

Security Architecture — the protective mechanisms, controls, and patterns that safeguard assets, 
operations, and trust

Integration Architecture — the patterns, protocols, and platforms that connect systems, data, and 
services across the enterprise

Cloud Architecture — the design of cloud services, deployment models, governance, and 
economics within the enterprise
North Star perspective: Understand how these domains connect rather than studying each as an 
isolated technical discipline.
A data architecture decision affects application design. An application choice affects integration 
complexity. An integration pattern affects security posture. A security requirement affects 
infrastructure design. An infrastructure constraint affects cloud strategy. A cloud strategy affects cost, 
agility, and vendor relationships. These connections are not incidental. They are the essence of 
architecture.
41

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 42
text:
The enterprise architect who optimizes one domain without understanding its ripple effects across the 
others builds excellence in isolation and fragility in the system. The enterprise architect who sees the 
connections makes decisions that strengthen the whole.
F3.3 — Business Architecture & Capabilities
Architecture begins with the business. Not with technology. Not with infrastructure. With the business.
Business capabilities are what the enterprise can reliably, repeatedly deliver to create value. Not what 
it intends to deliver. Not what it has delivered once. What it can deliver consistently, at scale, with 
quality. A capability is the combination of people, processes, technology, data, and knowledge that 
produces a business outcome.
Capabilities cross departments. "Customer onboarding" is a capability that touches sales, legal, finance, 
operations, and technology. "Product development" is a capability that touches research, engineering, 
marketing, supply chain, and quality. Mapping capabilities reveals where the enterprise is strong, 
where it is fragmented, and where technology investment will have the greatest impact.
Business processes are the sequences of activities that deliver capabilities. They are the "how" to 
capability's "what." Processes can be standardized or customized, manual or automated, simple or 
complex. Understanding processes reveals where technology can eliminate waste, accelerate flow, or 
enable new possibilities.
Operating models are the organisational choices that determine how capabilities are delivered: 
centralised or decentralized, insourced or outsourced, standardized or tailored. The operating model 
shapes technology requirements. A centralised operating model needs unified platforms. A 
decentralized model needs integration and federation.
Value streams trace the flow of value from initial stakeholder demand through to realised outcome. 
They cut across processes, departments, and systems. Value stream mapping reveals where technology 
accelerates value, where it blocks value, and where it is irrelevant.
Capability mapping is the practice of documenting the enterprise's capabilities, their maturity, their 
ownership, and their technology support. It is not an academic exercise. It is the foundation for 
investment prioritisation, transformation planning, and architectural decision-making.
Capability maturity describes how well a capability performs. Immature capabilities are ad hoc, 
inconsistent, and reactive. Mature capabilities are standardized, measured, optimised, and continuously 
improving. Technology investment should target capabilities where improved maturity will create the 
greatest strategic value.
Business–IT alignment in the architectural context means that technology investments are traceable to 
capability gaps, process improvements, or value stream enhancements. Architecture is the mechanism 
that makes this traceability visible and defensible.
Identifying capability gaps is where architecture creates strategic value. A gap exists when the 
enterprise needs a capability it does not have, or when an existing capability is too immature to support 
strategic objectives. Architecture translates these gaps into technology implications: new systems, 
integrations, data platforms, or infrastructure.
42

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 43
text:
F3.4 — Application & Solution Architecture
Applications are where business capabilities become operational reality. Application architecture is the 
discipline of ensuring that the application portfolio serves the enterprise coherently — not as a 
collection of isolated purchases, but as an integrated system of capabilities.
Application landscapes are the complete inventory of systems: what they do, who owns them, how 
they connect, how old they are, what they cost, and what risk they carry. Most enterprises do not truly 
know their application landscape. They know the major systems. They lose track of the shadow IT, the 
legacy remnants, the departmental tools, the abandoned pilots. Architecture demands visibility.
Systems of record are the authoritative sources of enterprise data: the ERP for financial and 
operational data, the CRM for customer data, the HRIS for workforce data. They are the foundation of 
truth. Without them, the enterprise operates on fragmented, inconsistent information.
Systems of engagement are the interfaces through which users — customers, employees, partners — 
interact with the enterprise: portals, mobile apps, websites, chatbots. They are where experience is 
shaped and value is realised.
Systems of intelligence are the analytics, AI, and decision-support systems that turn data into insight 
and insight into action. They are increasingly where competitive advantage is created.
ERP, CRM, HRIS, and enterprise platforms are the backbone systems that span the organisation. They 
are expensive, complex, and deeply embedded. Architectural decisions about these platforms — 
whether to upgrade, replace, customize, or standardize — have consequences that ripple across the 
enterprise for years.
Custom vs. COTS vs. SaaS is the fundamental application decision:

Custom development builds exactly what the enterprise needs. It offers differentiation, fit, and 
control. It also requires ongoing investment, specialized skills, and carries the full burden of 
maintenance, security, and evolution.

COTS (Commercial Off-The-Shelf) packages provide proven functionality, vendor support, and 
industry best practices. They require configuration, integration, and often compromise on exact fit.

SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers capability through subscription, with continuous updates, 
reduced operational burden, and rapid deployment. It offers less customization, creates vendor 
dependency, and requires careful data and integration governance.
There is no universal right answer. The right choice depends on strategic context: the importance of 
differentiation, the pace of change, the available skills, the risk tolerance, and the total cost over the 
lifecycle.
Application rationalization is the disciplined process of evaluating the application portfolio: 
identifying redundancy, assessing value, determining lifecycle position, and deciding whether to retain, 
consolidate, replace, or retire each application. It is essential hygiene. Without it, portfolios grow 
indefinitely, costs escalate, and agility erodes.
Technical debt in the application context is the accumulated cost of suboptimal design decisions: 
hardcoded integrations, insufficient testing, bypassed standards, deferred refactoring. It compounds. 
Every new feature built on fragile foundations increases the cost and risk of future change.
Buy vs. Build vs. Subscribe is not a one-time decision. It is a continuous evaluation. The right answer 
changes as markets mature, as vendor offerings improve, as enterprise needs evolve, and as internal 
43

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 44
text:
capabilities develop. Architecture provides the framework for making these evaluations consistently 
and transparently.
F3.5 — Data & Information Architecture
This section builds directly on the data concepts introduced in F2. If F2 established that data is an 
enterprise asset, F3 examines how that asset is architected.
Data domains are the logical categories of enterprise data: customer, product, financial, operational, 
employee, supplier, regulatory. Each domain has its own characteristics, ownership, quality 
requirements, and lifecycle. Organizing data by domain enables governance, reduces duplication, and 
clarifies accountability.
Data ownership is the business accountability for data quality, definition, access policy, and 
appropriate use. It is not an IT role. The CFO owns financial data definitions. The CMO owns customer 
data policies. The CHRO owns workforce data standards. IT enables. Business owns.
Data flows trace how data moves through the enterprise: where it originates, how it is transformed, 
where it is stored, who accesses it, and how it is consumed. Mapping data flows reveals integration 
requirements, security exposure, compliance obligations, and optimisation opportunities.
Master Data Management (MDM) is the discipline of maintaining a single, authoritative source for 
core reference data: customers, products, suppliers, locations, employees. Without MDM, the same 
entity exists in multiple systems with different identifiers, different attributes, and different levels of 
accuracy. Decisions become unreliable. Operations become inefficient. Compliance becomes impossible.
Data quality is the degree to which data is accurate, complete, consistent, timely, and fit for purpose. It 
is not a technical metric. It is a business metric that determines whether the enterprise can trust its 
decisions.
Data lifecycle is the journey from creation to deletion: capture, validate, store, process, analyse, share, 
archive, dispose. Each stage has architectural implications: storage performance, access controls, 
retention policies, compliance requirements, and cost.
Data governance is the framework of policies, standards, roles, and processes that ensure data is 
managed as an enterprise asset. It defines who can access what, how data is classified, how quality is 
maintained, and how compliance is assured. Governance without architecture is unenforceable. 
Architecture without governance is ungoverned.
Data platforms are the integrated environments that ingest, store, process, and serve data at scale. 
Modern platforms handle structured and unstructured data, batch and real-time processing, analytics 
and operational workloads, and AI training and inference.
Data lakes, warehouses, and lakehouses are the architectural patterns for enterprise data storage:

Data warehouses structure data for efficient querying and reporting. They are optimised for known 
questions and standardized schemas.

Data lakes store raw data in its native format, enabling flexible exploration and advanced analytics. 
They are optimised for discovery and experimentation.

Data lakehouses combine the flexibility of lakes with the structure and performance of 
warehouses. They are increasingly the default architecture for modern enterprises.
44

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 45
text:
Data as an enterprise asset is the governing principle. Data architecture is not about technology 
choice. It is about ensuring that the enterprise can trust, access, protect, and leverage its data to create 
value, manage risk, and comply with obligations.
F3.6 — Integration & API Architecture
Enterprise value increasingly depends on how well systems connect. Integration architecture is the 
discipline of designing those connections with coherence, security, and sustainability.
Why enterprise integration matters is simple: no enterprise operates with a single system. Even small 
organisations use dozens. Large enterprises use hundreds or thousands. These systems must exchange 
data, coordinate actions, and present unified experiences. Without integration, the enterprise is a 
collection of isolated silos. With poor integration, it is a fragile web of brittle connections. With good 
integration, it is a responsive, coherent system.
APIs (Application Programming Interfaces) are the contracts that define how systems communicate. 
They specify what data can be requested, what operations can be performed, and what responses will 
be returned. APIs are the language of modern enterprise connectivity. They are also the boundary of 
control: what you expose, how you secure it, and who can access it.
API gateways are the management layer that sits between API consumers and providers. They handle 
authentication, rate limiting, monitoring, versioning, and security. A gateway without governance is an 
open door. A gateway with governance is a controlled interface.
REST and event-driven integration are the two dominant patterns:

REST (Representational State Transfer) is the request-response pattern: a consumer asks, a 
provider answers. It is simple, synchronous, and well-understood. It is also blocking: the consumer 
waits for the response.

Event-driven integration is the publish-subscribe pattern: a producer announces that something 
happened, and interested consumers react independently. It is asynchronous, decoupled, and 
scalable. It is also more complex to design, monitor, and debug.
Messaging is the infrastructure that carries information between systems: queues, topics, buses, and 
brokers. Messaging provides reliability, scalability, and decoupling. It is the backbone of event-driven 
architecture.
ESB (Enterprise Service Bus) vs. modern integration represents an architectural evolution. ESBs 
were centralised integration platforms that mediated all system communication. They offered 
governance and consistency but became bottlenecks and single points of failure. Modern integration 
favors decentralized patterns: API gateways, event meshes, microservices communication, and cloud-
native integration platforms. The principle remains: integration must be governed. The practice has 
evolved toward greater flexibility and resilience.
Microservices and integration create both opportunity and complexity. Each microservice exposes 
APIs. Each API is a contract. Each contract must be versioned, secured, monitored, and evolved. The 
integration surface area expands dramatically. Architecture provides the patterns and governance to 
manage this expansion.
Synchronous vs. asynchronous communication is a fundamental design choice. Synchronous is 
simpler but creates dependencies and blocking. Asynchronous is more resilient but requires handling of 
45

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 46
text:
eventual consistency, failure scenarios, and complexity. The right choice depends on the business 
requirement, not technical preference.
Integration security ensures that connections between systems do not become pathways for attack. 
Every integration point is a potential vulnerability. Authentication, authorization, encryption, logging, 
and monitoring are essential.
Enterprise integration patterns are the reusable solutions to common integration challenges: routing, 
transformation, aggregation, splitting, error handling, idempotency. They are not technology-specific. 
They are architectural knowledge that transcends platforms.
F3.7 — Cloud & Hybrid Architecture
Cloud is not a destination. It is an architectural choice — about control, economics, agility, and risk — 
that must be aligned with enterprise strategy.
Public, private, and hybrid cloud are deployment models, not moral categories:

Public cloud is shared infrastructure owned by a provider, accessible over the internet. It offers 
scale, innovation, and operational flexibility. It also requires trust in the provider's security, 
compliance, and continuity.

Private cloud is dedicated infrastructure for a single organisation. It offers control, compliance, and 
customization. It also requires capital investment, operational expertise, and continuous 
maintenance.

Hybrid cloud combines both, with workloads placed according to requirements: sensitive data in 
private cloud, scalable services in public cloud, legacy systems on-premises. It offers flexibility but 
demands integration, governance, and operational sophistication.
IaaS, PaaS, and SaaS are service models that define where the boundary of responsibility lies:

IaaS — the provider manages infrastructure; the enterprise manages platforms, applications, and 
data

PaaS — the provider manages infrastructure and platform; the enterprise manages applications 
and data

SaaS — the provider manages everything; the enterprise consumes the application
The enterprise's responsibility decreases as it moves up the stack. Its dependency on the provider 
increases. Architecture defines where each workload belongs based on control requirements, 
compliance constraints, customization needs, and economic considerations.
Cloud-native architecture is the approach of designing applications specifically for cloud 
environments: microservices, containers, serverless, DevOps automation, elastic scaling. It maximizes 
cloud benefits but requires new skills, new governance, and new ways of working.
Multi-cloud is the use of multiple cloud providers to avoid vendor lock-in, optimise capabilities, and 
increase resilience. It offers choice but multiplies complexity: different interfaces, different security 
models, different cost structures, different compliance regimes.
Hybrid integration connects cloud and on-premises systems, cloud-to-cloud systems, and legacy-to-
modern systems. It is the reality of most enterprises and one of the most challenging architectural 
domains.
46

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 47
text:
Cloud governance ensures that cloud usage is consistent, secure, compliant, and cost-effective. It 
includes policies for provisioning, tagging, access, encryption, networking, and data residency. Without 
governance, cloud becomes an uncontrolled expense and an unmonitored risk.
Cloud economics / FinOps is the practice of managing cloud costs with the same discipline as 
traditional IT financial management. It requires visibility into usage, accountability for spending, 
optimisation of resources, and continuous monitoring. Cloud's pay-as-you-go model is powerful but 
dangerous without financial discipline.
Portability and vendor lock-in are the strategic risks of cloud dependency. The more an enterprise 
uses provider-specific services, the harder it becomes to move workloads elsewhere. Architecture must 
balance the benefits of native services against the risk of future inflexibility.
Cloud migration architecture is the planned transition of workloads from on-premises to cloud. It is 
not a single event. It is a sequence of decisions: which workloads to move, in what order, using what 
approach (rehost, replatform, refactor, rebuild, retire), with what governance, and toward what target 
state.
F3.8 — Security Architecture by Design
Security is not a separate technical function. It is an architectural discipline — woven into every layer, 
every decision, every connection.
Security by Design means that security is considered from the first moment of architectural thinking, 
not added as an afterthought. It is cheaper, more effective, and more sustainable than retrofitting 
security onto systems that were built without it.
Zero Trust principles reject the assumption that anything inside the network is safe. Every access 
request is verified. Every user is authenticated. Every device is validated. Every transaction is 
authorised. Trust is never assumed. It is continuously earned.
Identity-centric architecture places identity at the center of security. Who you are determines what 
you can access. Identity is the perimeter. Identity management, authentication, and authorization are 
not afterthoughts. They are foundational architectural services.
Network segmentation divides the enterprise network into zones, limiting the lateral movement of 
attackers. It is not merely a technical configuration. It is an architectural decision about how the 
enterprise organizes its technology for resilience.
Data protection ensures that data is secure at rest, in transit, and in use. Encryption, access controls, 
masking, and tokenization are architectural choices about how the enterprise values and protects its 
information assets.
Application security embeds security into the software lifecycle: secure coding, vulnerability scanning, 
penetration testing, dependency management. It is not a checkpoint before deployment. It is a 
continuous discipline.
Security architecture patterns are the reusable approaches to common security challenges: defense in 
depth, least privilege, separation of duties, defense in breadth. They are not technology-specific. They 
are principles that guide technology choice.
47

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 48
text:
Resilience and recovery ensure that security incidents do not become business catastrophes. Backup, 
redundancy, failover, and incident response are architectural decisions about how the enterprise 
survives failure.
Privacy by Design ensures that personal data is protected by default. Data minimization, purpose 
limitation, transparency, and user control are not compliance checkboxes. They are architectural 
commitments to ethical technology.
F3.9 — Architecture Governance & Decision-Making
This is a particularly important executive section. Read it carefully.
Architecture without governance is aspiration. Governance without architecture is bureaucracy. The 
discipline is in combining them.
Architecture principles are the enduring rules that guide decisions across time and initiatives. They 
are not detailed standards. They are directional commitments: "Cloud-first for new applications." "API-
first for system integration." "Security by design, not by inspection." "Buy before build unless 
differentiation requires custom development." Principles must be few, clear, and consistently applied. 
Too many principles become noise. Too vague principles become meaningless.
Architecture standards are the specific implementations of principles: approved technology platforms, 
mandated integration patterns, required security controls, defined data formats. Standards provide 
consistency. They also constrain choice. The discipline is in maintaining standards that are current, 
relevant, and enforced — while allowing exceptions when justified.
Architecture Review Board is the governance body that evaluates significant technology decisions 
against architecture principles and standards. It is not a bottleneck. It is a quality mechanism. Its 
effectiveness depends on its authority, its speed, and its credibility. A review board that takes months to 
approve decisions destroys agility. A review board that rubber-stamps everything destroys architecture.
Technology standards define what the enterprise uses, why, and under what conditions. They reduce 
duplication, leverage scale, and simplify support. They also risk creating rigidity. The enterprise must 
balance standardisation with the flexibility to adopt innovations that create competitive advantage.
Exceptions and waivers are the safety valve. No set of principles and standards can anticipate every 
situation. The discipline is in documenting exceptions, understanding their implications, and ensuring 
they do not become the norm. An architecture with too many exceptions has no architecture.
Technical debt governance is the practice of tracking, measuring, and managing the accumulated cost 
of suboptimal decisions. It requires visibility: where debt exists, what it costs, what it risks, and what it 
would take to reduce it. Technical debt is not inherently bad. It is a strategic choice to borrow capability 
from the future. But it must be borrowed knowingly and repaid deliberately.
Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) document why significant decisions were made: the context, 
the options considered, the trade-offs evaluated, the decision taken, and the consequences accepted. 
They provide organisational memory. They enable future architects to understand the reasoning behind 
the current state. They prevent the same debates from recurring endlessly.
Risk-based architecture decisions weigh the probability and impact of failure against the cost and 
benefit of mitigation. Not every system requires the same level of architectural rigor. A customer-facing 
48

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 49
text:
transaction system demands exhaustive review. An internal reporting tool may not. Architecture 
governance must be proportionate.
Governance vs. bureaucracy is the eternal tension. Governance ensures quality, consistency, and 
sustainability. Bureaucracy ensures delay, frustration, and evasion. The difference lies in speed, 
proportionality, and trust. Governance that takes weeks to approve a minor change is bureaucracy. 
Governance that provides clear criteria, rapid feedback, and transparent rationale is architecture.
F3.10 — Architecture Frameworks & Standards
The IT profession has produced remarkable frameworks for architecture. North Star does not replace 
them. It connects and contextualizes them.
TOGAF (The Open Group Architecture Framework) is the most widely adopted enterprise 
architecture methodology. It provides a structured approach to developing architecture: vision, 
business architecture, information systems architecture, technology architecture, opportunities and 
solutions, migration planning, implementation governance, and architecture change management. 
TOGAF is comprehensive. It is also complex. North Star does not teach TOGAF. It teaches you when 
TOGAF adds value and when simpler approaches suffice.
ArchiMate is the modeling language for enterprise architecture. It provides a standardized way to 
represent business processes, organisational structures, information flows, system landscapes, and 
technology infrastructure. It is a communication tool. Its value lies in creating shared understanding. Its 
risk lies in becoming an end in itself — beautiful diagrams that no one uses.
COBIT provides a framework for the governance and management of enterprise information and 
technology. It connects stakeholder needs and enterprise objectives with governance and management 
objectives, practices, information, people, skills, policies, processes, and technology. Architecture can 
operate within this governance system, but COBIT does not prescribe how to design individual 
solutions.
ITIL provides best-practice guidance for managing digital products and services. It helps connect 
architecture decisions to service value, operational support, change, incident resolution, continual 
improvement, and the wider service-management system. Architecture should therefore consider how 
solutions will be operated and supported throughout their lifecycle.
NIST develops cybersecurity standards, guidelines, frameworks, and supporting resources. The 
Cybersecurity Framework, in particular, provides outcomes for governing and managing cybersecurity 
risk that can inform security architecture, assessment, prioritisation, and improvement.
ISO/IEC 27001 specifies requirements for establishing, implementing, maintaining, and continually 
improving an information security management system. It is not an architecture framework, but its 
risk-based management-system requirements influence security governance, control selection, 
assurance, and the architectural decisions needed to support them.
ISO/IEC 20000-1 specifies requirements for a service management system. It is not an architecture 
framework, but its service-management requirements influence how architecture supports service 
quality, continuity, control, and customer value.
Relationship between frameworks: No single framework covers everything. TOGAF provides a 
framework for enterprise architecture; COBIT integrates governance with management of enterprise 
information and technology; ITIL guides service and product management; NIST offers cybersecurity,

and, where relevant, have independently certified. The enterprise architect should understand where 
each fits, how they overlap, and when each is useful.

When to use which framework depends on context. A large, regulated enterprise with complex legacy

applying the most comprehensive framework to every situation.
North Star does not teach these frameworks in depth. It teaches you to navigate them: to know what 
they offer, where they fit, and how to use them as tools rather than constraints.
F3.11 — Modern Architecture Patterns
The executive does not need to design systems. The executive needs to recognise the concepts, 
understand their business implications, and ask the right questions.
Monolith vs. modular architecture is the foundational choice. A monolith is a single, unified 
application where all components are tightly coupled. It is simpler to develop and deploy but harder to 
change, scale, and maintain. A modular architecture separates components into independent units. It is 
more complex to design but more flexible, resilient, and scalable.
Microservices are an architectural pattern where applications are built as small, independent services 
that communicate through APIs. Each service can be developed, deployed, and scaled independently. 
This enables agility and resilience but increases operational complexity, integration surface area, and 
governance requirements.
50

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 51
text:
Event-driven architecture is the pattern where systems communicate through events rather than 
direct requests. It enables real-time responsiveness, loose coupling, and scalability. It also requires 
careful handling of consistency, failure, and observability.
API-first is the discipline of designing APIs before building the systems that consume or provide them. 
It ensures that integration is intentional, contracts are clear, and consumers are considered from the 
beginning.
Cloud-native is the approach of designing applications specifically for cloud environments: containers, 
microservices, DevOps, elastic scaling, and automated management. It maximizes cloud benefits but 
requires new skills, tools, and governance.
Containerization packages applications with their dependencies into portable units that can run 
consistently across environments. It enables flexibility, scalability, and efficient resource use.
Kubernetes is the platform for automating the deployment, scaling, and management of containerized 
applications. It is powerful and complex. It is not a requirement for every enterprise, but it is 
increasingly the standard for cloud-native operations.
Platform engineering is the discipline of building internal platforms that provide developers with self-
service tools, standardized environments, and governed pathways. It reduces friction, increases 
consistency, and accelerates delivery.
DevSecOps integrates security into the DevOps pipeline: automated security testing, vulnerability 
scanning, compliance checks, and threat modeling as part of every build and deployment. It is security 
by design, operationalized.
Serverless is the model where the enterprise writes code without managing the underlying 
infrastructure. The cloud provider handles provisioning, scaling, and maintenance. It offers simplicity 
and cost efficiency for event-driven, variable workloads.
Composable architecture is the approach of building systems from interchangeable, modular 
components that can be assembled, reassembled, and replaced as needs change. It enables business 
agility by making technology more adaptable.
The executive question for each pattern is not "How does it work?" but "What does it enable, what does it 
require, and what does it risk?"
F3.12 — Architecture & AI
This section creates the bridge from F2's AI foundations toward future transformation topics.
AI-ready enterprise architecture is not about adding AI to existing systems. It is about designing the 
enterprise so that AI can be adopted responsibly, scalably, and effectively. It requires data foundations, 
integration patterns, infrastructure elasticity, governance mechanisms, and human oversight.
AI workloads and infrastructure demand specialized resources: high-performance compute, GPU 
clusters, large-scale storage, low-latency networks, and elastic scaling. These are architectural decisions 
about capacity, cost, and location.
Data foundations for AI are the prerequisite for any meaningful AI deployment. Without clean, 
governed, accessible data, AI produces noise, not insight. Architecture must ensure that data is 
discoverable, quality-assured, properly labeled, and appropriately protected.
51

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 52
text:
AI integration patterns define how AI services connect to enterprise systems: embedded in 
applications, exposed through APIs, deployed as standalone services, or orchestrated through AI 
platforms. Each pattern has implications for latency, security, scalability, and governance.
APIs and AI services are the interface layer. AI capabilities — language models, vision models, 
recommendation engines — are consumed as services. The architecture must manage authentication, 
rate limiting, monitoring, versioning, and fallback.
RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) architecture combines large language models with 
enterprise knowledge bases. It enables AI to generate responses grounded in the organisation's own 
data. It requires vector databases, embedding pipelines, retrieval mechanisms, and careful governance 
of what the AI can and cannot access.
AI agents and enterprise systems represent the frontier: autonomous or semi-autonomous systems 
that plan, execute multi-step tasks, and interact with other systems on behalf of users. They require 
robust integration, clear boundaries, human oversight, and fail-safe mechanisms.
AI governance architecture defines who decides what AI can do, how its decisions are monitored, how 
bias is detected, how errors are handled, and how accountability is maintained. It is not a technical 
layer. It is an architectural commitment to responsible AI.
Human-in-the-loop is the architectural pattern that ensures human judgment remains part of AI-
driven processes. It defines where humans review, approve, override, or intervene. It is essential for 
high-stakes decisions and regulatory compliance.
AI security and privacy address the unique risks of AI: model inversion attacks, prompt injection, data 
poisoning, hallucination, and unintended disclosure of sensitive information. Architecture must protect 
AI systems as rigorously as it protects any other enterprise asset.
AI platform strategy is the decision about whether to build, buy, or partner for AI capabilities. It 
involves evaluating cloud AI services, open-source models, proprietary platforms, and hybrid 
approaches. The architecture must support the chosen strategy without creating unmanageable 
fragmentation.
F3.13 — Technology Strategy & Architecture Roadmaps
Architecture is not a destination. It is a journey from current state to target state, navigated through 
disciplined decisions and sequenced investments.
Current State is the honest assessment of what exists: systems, integrations, data, infrastructure, skills, 
costs, risks, and technical debt. It is not what the architecture documents say exists. It is what actually 
exists, measured and verified.
Target State is the envisioned future: the technology landscape that enables the enterprise's strategic 
objectives. It is not a fantasy. It is a coherent, achievable, and justified picture of where the architecture 
needs to go.
Gap Analysis is the disciplined comparison between current and target states. It identifies what is 
missing, what is redundant, what is misaligned, and what must change. It quantifies the distance 
between aspiration and reality.
52

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 53
text:
Transition Architecture is the interim state: the coherent, stable configuration that the enterprise 
passes through on its way to the target. It is not a holding pattern. It is a deliberate, governed state that 
maintains operations while enabling progress.
Architecture Roadmap is the sequence of initiatives, investments, and decisions that moves the 
enterprise from current to target state. It includes timelines, dependencies, resource requirements, risk 
mitigations, and decision points. It is not a project plan. It is a strategic guide that informs project 
planning.
Technology modernisation is the continuous effort to update, replace, or retire systems that no longer 
serve the enterprise effectively. It is not a one-time programme. It is a permanent discipline.
Legacy transformation is the specific challenge of dealing with deeply embedded, often critical, 
systems that are costly to maintain and risky to change. It requires careful analysis, staged migration, 
and sometimes creative alternatives: encapsulation, replacement, or acceptance.
Prioritisation in the roadmap is not about what is easiest or most urgent. It is about what creates the 
most strategic value with acceptable risk and feasible investment. It balances quick wins that build 
momentum with foundational investments that enable future capability.
Dependencies are the relationships between initiatives: technical dependencies, resource 
dependencies, business dependencies, and regulatory dependencies. Understanding dependencies 
prevents the roadmap from becoming a wish list.
Investment sequencing is the order in which the enterprise commits resources. It considers cash flow, 
risk reduction, capability building, and strategic timing. Sequencing is where architecture meets 
finance.
Business value vs. technical complexity is the fundamental trade-off in roadmap decisions. High-
value, low-complexity initiatives are the quick wins. High-value, high-complexity initiatives are the 
strategic bets. Low-value, low-complexity initiatives are the maintenance. Low-value, high-complexity 
initiatives are the traps.
F3.14 — Architecture Decisions at Executive Level
This is a practical executive decision framework. Use it.
The dimensions are:
Business Value 
 Risk 
 Cost 
 Complexity 
 Capability 
 Time 
 Strategic Fit
→
→
→
→
→
→
Business Value — What outcome does this decision enable? Revenue growth? Cost reduction? Risk 
mitigation? Customer experience? Competitive differentiation? Value must be specific, measurable, and 
traceable to strategic objectives.
Risk — What could go wrong? Security breach? Operational failure? Vendor collapse? Skill shortage? 
Regulatory non-compliance? Cost overrun? Risk must be identified, quantified where possible, and 
mitigated deliberately.
Cost — What is the total cost of ownership, not merely the purchase price? Licensing, implementation, 
integration, training, maintenance, support, retirement? Cost must be evaluated over the full lifecycle.
53

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 54
text:
Complexity — How difficult is this to execute? Technical complexity? Organisational complexity? 
Integration complexity? Cultural complexity? Complexity consumes resources, extends timelines, and 
increases failure probability.
Capability — Does this build something the enterprise needs? Does it close a gap? Does it create 
differentiation? Does it enable future options? Capability must be evaluated against current and future 
requirements.
Time — How long until value is realised? Quick wins sustain momentum. Long-term investments build 
foundations. The portfolio must balance both.
Strategic Fit — Does this align with where the enterprise is going? Does it support the business model? 
Does it enable the operating model? Does it differentiate or commoditize?
Decisions such as:

Replace vs. modernize — Replace when the system cannot meet future requirements, the cost of 
maintenance exceeds replacement, or the risk of failure is unacceptable. Modernize when the core 
system remains viable but needs updating.

Build vs. buy — Build when the capability is strategic, unique, and differentiating. Buy when the 
market offers mature, proven solutions.

Cloud vs. on-premises — Cloud when agility, scalability, and innovation speed matter most. On-
premises when control, compliance, and predictability are paramount.

Centralise vs. decentralize — Centralise when standardisation, efficiency, and governance are 
critical. Decentralize when speed, innovation, and local ownership matter more.

Best-of-breed vs. integrated platform — Best-of-breed when each function demands specialized 
excellence. Integrated platform when coherence, simplicity, and unified data are paramount.

Single vendor vs. multi-vendor — Single vendor when integration, accountability, and 
relationship depth matter. Multi-vendor when avoiding lock-in, optimizing capabilities, and 
maintaining leverage are critical.

Customization vs. standardisation — Customize when competitive differentiation requires it. 
Standardize when operational efficiency and maintainability are paramount.

Innovation vs. stability — Innovate when the market demands it and the organisation can absorb 
the risk. Stabilize when operational reliability is the priority.
There is no universal right answer to any of these. There is only the answer that fits the enterprise's 
context, strategy, and constraints.
F3.15 — Executive Architecture Case Study
This section brings F3 together through a complete scenario. Read it as an exercise in applying 
everything this chapter has established.
The situation:
A government organisation has fragmented applications, aging infrastructure, duplicated data, weak 
integration, increasing cybersecurity risk, and pressure to introduce AI.
The learner must determine:

Current-state architecture — What exists, what works, what fails, what costs, what risks

Business capability gaps — Where the organisation cannot deliver what its mission requires
54

title: Enterprise Architecture & Technology Design — page 55
text:

Application rationalization — Which systems to retain, consolidate, replace, or retire

Data architecture direction — How to unify, govern, and leverage data as an enterprise asset

Integration strategy — How to connect systems coherently without creating fragility

Cloud / hybrid strategy — Where workloads belong, how to migrate, and how to govern

Security architecture — How to protect assets, ensure resilience, and comply with obligations

Target architecture — The envisioned future state that enables the mission

Transformation roadmap — The sequenced path from current to target

Governance model — How architecture decisions will be made, reviewed, and enforced

Investment priorities — Where resources should flow first, and why

Executive recommendation — What the leadership should decide, with clear rationale
This case study is not a test. It is a practice ground. The answers are less important than the reasoning. 
The discipline of working through each dimension — understanding the current state, envisioning the 
target, analysing gaps, designing transitions, sequencing investments, and governing execution — is the 
architecture mindset North Star seeks to develop.
F3 — Reader Outcome
By the end of F3, you should be able to:


How business strategy, capabilities, and technology architecture connect.

The major architecture domains and their relationships.

How architecture frameworks, patterns, and governance work together.
Decide



When to build, buy, modernize, or retire.

How to balance standardisation with innovation, and governance with agility.
Do

Translate business capability requirements into architectural considerations.

Engage architects, engineers, and vendors with informed, relevant questions.

Contribute to architecture governance as an executive leader.

Assess whether a technology landscape enables strategy or merely accumulates complexity.
