title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 82
text:
Dependencies and resource allocation
Dependencies between projects, programmes, suppliers, operational teams, and external authorities 
must be visible and actively managed. Resource allocation must reflect actual skills and capacity, not 
optimistic assumptions.
Benefits management
Benefits management establishes baselines, targets, ownership, measurement, and follow-up so that 
promised outcomes are not lost after delivery.
Executive oversight
Senior leadership should remain actively engaged in material decisions, trade-offs, risk acceptance, and 
portfolio prioritisation. Executive oversight is not ceremonial status review; it is informed decision-
making.
F5.4 — Delivery Approaches & Methodologies
The delivery method should serve the nature of the work. No single methodology is universally correct.
Predictive
Predictive or plan-driven delivery works well where requirements are stable, outcomes are understood, 
change is costly, and formal sequencing or compliance is important.
Agile
Agile delivery uses short feedback cycles, incremental value, customer collaboration, and adaptation. It 
is valuable where uncertainty is high and learning is essential. Agile without discipline is not agility; it is 
uncontrolled change.
Hybrid
Hybrid delivery combines predictive and adaptive approaches where an initiative contains both stable 
and uncertain components. This is common in enterprise technology.
Iterative and incremental delivery
Iterative delivery refines the solution through repeated cycles. Incremental delivery releases usable 
capability in smaller pieces. The two can be combined.
Product-oriented delivery
Product thinking treats a capability as something that requires continuous ownership, investment, 
improvement, and eventual retirement rather than a one-time project.
DevOps and DevSecOps
DevOps integrates development and operations to improve delivery flow and reliability. DevSecOps 
embeds security into that flow. Both require appropriate automation, skills, controls, and culture.
82

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 83
text:
Choosing the approach

What is the degree of uncertainty?

What is the tolerance for change and risk?

How stable are the requirements?

What regulatory or assurance constraints apply?

What delivery capability exists?

How urgent is the outcome?

What level of predictability is required?
Methodology should serve the nature of the work — not the other way around.
F5.5 — Project Initiation & Business Case
Before delivery begins, the executive must understand why the initiative should exist. Initiation is the 
discipline of committing resources to purpose rather than preference.

Business problem — the measurable current-state pain, gap, risk, or opportunity.

Strategic alignment — why solving the problem supports enterprise direction.

Objectives — what the initiative intends to achieve.

Scope — what is included, excluded, deferred, and assumed.

Expected outcomes — measurable changes the business expects.

Benefits — quantified or otherwise defined value resulting from those outcomes.

Options analysis — build, buy, outsource, partner, or do nothing.

Cost and investment — total financial, human, operational, and opportunity cost.

Risks — uncertainties that could affect delivery or value.

Assumptions — conditions believed to be true for the case to hold.

Constraints — limits such as budget, regulation, skills, timing, or technology.

Feasibility — technical, organisational, financial, operational, and strategic viability.
Business case
The business case is a decision tool, not a sales pitch. It should allow decision-makers to understand the 
problem, alternatives, investment, risks, expected benefits, and consequences of action or inaction.
Project charter and authorization
Initiation documentation formally establishes purpose, scope, accountability, governance, resources, 
constraints, and decision rights. It creates the authority for delivery to proceed.
Go / No-Go
A clear decision should authorize, defer, reshape, or reject the initiative. Continuing without explicit 
authority creates accountability and investment ambiguity.
F5.6 — Scope, Requirements & Expectations
Scope is a disciplined agreement about what the project will deliver, what it will not deliver, and what 
success looks like.
83

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 84
text:
Scope and requirements
Scope defines project boundaries. Requirements define what the solution must provide. Requirements 
should be clear, testable, traceable, and connected to business objectives.
Business, functional and non-functional requirements
Business requirements express business needs and outcomes. Functional requirements describe what a 
solution does. Non-functional requirements describe qualities such as performance, reliability, security, 
usability, scalability, and maintainability.
Acceptance criteria
Acceptance criteria define the conditions under which stakeholders will accept a deliverable. They 
should be measurable and agreed early enough to guide delivery.
Scope boundaries
Explicit exclusions, deferred items, assumptions, and constraints protect delivery from ambiguity and 
uncontrolled expansion.
Scope creep and change control
Scope creep is uncontrolled expansion without corresponding adjustment to time, cost, quality, 
resources, or risk. Legitimate change should not be suppressed; it should be assessed, approved, 
resourced, baselined, and communicated.
Requirement traceability
Traceability links requirements to objectives, solution elements, tests, and acceptance criteria. It 
provides evidence that what was requested was actually built and verified.
Stakeholder expectations
Stakeholders judge delivery against what they believe was promised. Expectation management 
therefore requires continuous communication about scope, timing, quality, assumptions, and trade-offs.
What are we actually committing to deliver — and what are we explicitly not delivering?
F5.7 — Project Planning, Scheduling & Dependencies
A schedule is not a plan. Planning is the disciplined thinking that produces a coherent, achievable, and 
governable path from initiation to delivery.

Work breakdown — decomposing delivery into manageable components and deliverables.

Activities — the actions required to produce those deliverables.

Milestones — significant points that demonstrate achievement of a defined state.

Critical path — the sequence that determines the minimum achievable duration.

Dependencies — relationships between activities, projects, suppliers, approvals, and external 
factors.

Resource planning — matching required skills and capacity to delivery needs.

Capacity — the honest assessment of what the organisation can actually deliver.

Scheduling — sequencing work against dependencies, resources, and milestones.
84

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 85
text:

Baselines — approved scope, schedule, and cost references used for variance and change control.

Integrated planning — bringing scope, schedule, resources, risks, and dependencies into one 
coherent view.
Programme management adds another layer of dependency management across projects and 
operational changes.
A busy schedule is not evidence of an achievable plan.
F5.8 — Project Financial Management
Financial discipline in delivery is the continuous alignment of investment to value.
CAPEX and OPEX
CAPEX generally relates to investment in assets or capabilities with future benefit, while OPEX relates to 
ongoing operating costs. Cloud, SaaS, subscriptions, and managed services can shift technology 
economics toward recurring expenditure, changing how investments should be evaluated.
Budget, forecast and actuals
The budget is the approved allocation. The forecast is the current estimate of final cost. Actuals are what 
has been spent. The relationship among them provides early warning of financial drift.
Financial controls
Approval thresholds, expenditure tracking, invoice validation, contract compliance, and segregation of 
duties protect investment and reduce financial leakage.
Vendor and lifecycle cost
Technology cost includes acquisition, implementation, integration, customization, training, support, 
renewal, migration, and retirement. Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) is therefore often more meaningful 
than purchase price alone.
Contingency
Contingency is a governed reserve for identified uncertainty. It is not an unrestricted pool for 
unapproved scope.
ROI and strategic value
ROI is useful where financial returns can be credibly quantified. Some initiatives also create 
compliance, resilience, strategic optionality, or risk reduction that cannot be represented fully through 
simple ROI.
Benefits realisation
Financial and non-financial benefits should have baselines, targets, owners, measurement methods, and 
review points.
Budget ≠ Cost ≠ Investment ≠ Value
85

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 86
text:
F5.9 — Project Risk, Issues & Dependencies
F5 focuses here on risks that can affect delivery execution. Enterprise-wide risk, cybersecurity, 
resilience, and specialized control domains are addressed in their respective North Star chapters.
Risk vs. issue
A risk is a potential future event or condition that could affect objectives. An issue is a problem that has 
already occurred and requires action.
Risk identification and assessment
Delivery risks may include technical failure, vendor underperformance, resource loss, regulatory 
change, integration failure, scope expansion, schedule delay, cost overrun, and business readiness gaps. 
Assessment considers probability, impact, proximity, and response urgency.
Risk response

Avoid — change the plan so the risk no longer applies.

Mitigate — reduce probability or impact.

Transfer — allocate consequence to another party through appropriate contractual, insurance, or 
sourcing mechanisms.

Accept — consciously retain the risk with appropriate monitoring and contingency.
Risk ownership
Every material risk should have a named owner with the authority and capability to manage the 
response.
Issue management
Issues require clear ownership, impact assessment, options, decisions, action tracking, and escalation 
when authority or capability is exceeded.
Dependencies and assumptions
Dependencies create exposure when delivery relies on another activity, team, project, supplier, 
approval, or external condition. Assumptions should be tested because a failed assumption can become 
a material risk.
Escalation
Escalation is a control mechanism, not a sign of failure. Issues should be escalated early enough for 
leaders to retain meaningful choices.
Identify 
 Assess 
 Respond 
 Monitor 
 Escalate
→
→
→
→
F5.10 — Quality, Assurance & Acceptance
Quality is not an attribute tested only at the end. It is a discipline embedded throughout delivery.
86

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 87
text:
Quality management
Quality management establishes criteria, methods, assurance activities, testing, defect control, 
acceptance, and improvement.
Testing

Functional testing — verifies required behaviour.

Integration testing — verifies interfaces, data flows, events, and error handling.

Performance testing — verifies response, throughput, scalability, and stability.

Security testing — verifies security requirements and resistance to relevant threats.

User acceptance testing — verifies that the solution meets real business needs.
Defect management
Defects should be triaged according to severity, business impact, risk, and release criteria. Not every 
defect requires the same response.
Quality assurance vs. quality control
Quality assurance is primarily preventive: standards, reviews, process discipline, audits, and 
improvement. Quality control is primarily detective: testing, inspection, and verification.
Independent assurance
Independent assurance provides objective confidence that delivery, governance, risk management, and 
readiness are adequate. Independence strengthens credibility.
Go-live readiness
Readiness should consider functional completeness, quality, security, performance, documentation, 
training, operational support, monitoring, business acceptance, and rollback or contingency 
arrangements.
Quality ≠ Testing Alone
F5.11 — Vendors, Procurement & Commercial Delivery
F5 covers commercial delivery and procurement. F6 covers ongoing operational supplier performance. 
F7 covers supplier risk and security. F8 covers strategic vendor governance and ecosystem 
management.
External suppliers can provide critical capability, but vendor dependency must be governed as an 
enterprise delivery consideration.
Make vs. buy
Build when the capability is strategic, differentiating, or unavailable in a mature market. Buy when 
proven external capability can deliver better value, speed, or maintainability. The decision should 
consider strategic control and lifecycle implications.
Procurement mechanisms

RFI — gathers market information and supplier capability.
87

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 88
text:

RFP — solicits and evaluates proposed solutions.

RFQ — requests pricing for defined requirements.
Vendor selection
Selection should consider technical capability, financial stability, references, security, regulatory fit, 
delivery capability, commercial terms, cultural fit, and total cost of ownership.
Contract and SOW management
Contracts establish commercial obligations. Statements of Work define specific scope, deliverables, 
timelines, acceptance criteria, and responsibilities. Change control protects both parties from 
uncontrolled commercial drift.
SLA and KPI management
SLAs define service commitments. KPIs measure performance. Both should be linked to business 
expectations and governed through evidence.
Vendor dependency and commercial risk
Single-supplier dependency, weak knowledge transfer, proprietary technology, escalating renewal 
costs, poor exit terms, and vendor concentration can create long-term risk.
Exit strategy
Every material supplier relationship should have an exit approach covering data retrieval, intellectual 
property, knowledge transfer, transition support, continuity, licensing, and contractual obligations.
The moment you need an exit strategy is too late to create one.
F5.12 — Stakeholder & Delivery Leadership
Delivery happens through relationships, decisions, expectations, and influence. Technical competence 
alone does not guarantee successful execution.
Stakeholder identification and influence
Stakeholders include sponsors, users, customers, suppliers, regulators, auditors, operational teams, and 
other affected parties. Their influence, interest, concerns, and decision rights should be understood and 
revisited as delivery evolves.
Communication
Effective delivery communication is two-way. It surfaces progress, risks, concerns, decisions, trade-offs, 
and changing expectations. Communication should be timely, honest, tailored, and actionable.
Executive reporting
Executives need concise information on delivery health, decisions required, risk, issues, financial 
position, strategic alignment, and forecast — not a catalogue of activities.
88

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 89
text:
Steering committees
Steering committees should make decisions, resolve escalated matters, challenge delivery assumptions, 
and hold accountable leaders to account. They should not become passive status meetings.
Conflict and difficult stakeholders
Conflict may arise from legitimate competing priorities, risk concerns, resource constraints, or personal 
interests. Effective leadership seeks to understand the underlying issue, establish evidence, align on 
outcomes, and escalate when necessary.
Cross-functional ownership
Business, technology, operations, finance, security, procurement, and other disciplines should 
collaborate around shared outcomes. Business stakeholders are co-owners of benefits, not merely 
recipients of technology.
Escalation is not failure. It is the mechanism for resolving what cannot be resolved at lower 
levels.
F5.13 — Agile Delivery & Product Thinking
Agile is not the absence of governance. It is a different way of governing delivery.
Agile mindset
Agile emphasizes customer value, collaboration, working increments, feedback, and adaptation. It does 
not eliminate planning, documentation, contracts, controls, or accountability.
Product ownership
Product ownership is accountability for product direction, value, prioritisation, and customer outcomes. 
The product owner is not simply a project administrator.
Product vision and backlog
Product vision defines the intended value and direction. The backlog is a prioritised inventory of 
features, fixes, improvements, and technical work. It is not a fixed promise of everything that will ever 
be delivered.
User stories and prioritisation
User stories express needs from the user’s perspective and connect capability to value. Prioritisation is 
continuous and should reflect value, risk, dependencies, learning, and capacity.
Sprints and increments
A sprint is a time-boxed delivery cycle. An increment is a usable, tested result produced through 
delivery. The exact cadence and framework may vary.
MVP
A Minimum Viable Product is the smallest real product capable of testing important assumptions with 
real users. It is not merely a prototype.
89

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 90
text:
Product lifecycle
Product thinking extends beyond initial release through growth, maturity, optimisation, and retirement.
Product vs. project mindset
Project thinking asks when a defined initiative will finish. Product thinking asks how a capability will 
continuously create and improve value.
Agile governance
Agile governance maintains strategic alignment, financial discipline, risk management, quality, security, 
regulatory compliance, and accountability while enabling rapid feedback and flow.
Agile metrics
Useful measures may include throughput, cycle time, work in progress, defect trends, customer 
satisfaction, product adoption, and business outcomes. Velocity can support team planning, but it is not 
a direct measure of productivity or business value.
Agile is not the absence of governance. It is a different way of governing delivery.
F5.14 — Delivery Governance & Reporting
Governance ensures delivery remains aligned, controlled, transparent, accountable, and capable of 
achieving intended outcomes. Reporting provides the management information required to make 
decisions.
Project and programme governance
Project governance focuses on delivery control and accountability. Programme governance adds 
coordination, dependencies, integration, and benefits. Portfolio governance optimizes investment and 
strategic value.
Stage gates
Stage gates are evidence-based decision points at which leaders determine whether an initiative should 
proceed, change, pause, or stop. The evidence should reflect the nature of the delivery approach.
Decision rights
Decision rights clarify who can approve scope changes, funding, schedule changes, risk acceptance, 
vendor decisions, quality exceptions, and major technical or business choices.
RAG status
Red, Amber, Green status is useful only when it is evidence-based. A project that is green on schedule 
but red on material risk should not be presented as simply green.
RAID management
RAID provides a practical operational view of Risks, Assumptions, Issues, and Dependencies. It supports 
proactive governance but does not replace judgment.
90

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 91
text:
Change control
Change control ensures that changes to scope, schedule, cost, quality, or risk are assessed, approved, 
resourced, baselined where appropriate, and communicated.
Assurance
Assurance provides objective confidence that governance, delivery, risk, quality, readiness, and benefits 
mechanisms are functioning as intended.
Governance cadence
Different levels require different rhythms: operational team reviews may be frequent, project 
governance periodic, programme governance broader, and portfolio reviews focused on strategic 
investment and capacity.
Executive dashboards
Executive dashboards should highlight delivery health, material risk, financial position, strategic 
alignment, decisions required, and trends. They should reduce noise rather than increase it.
Reporting activity describes what happened. Management information enables leaders to decide 
what should happen next.
F5.15 — Project Performance & Delivery Metrics
Measurement is the discipline of understanding whether delivery is progressing, whether risks are 
changing, and whether the investment is producing the intended results.
Delivery performance

Schedule — milestone performance, critical path, forecast dates and variance.

Cost — budget, actuals, forecast at completion and cost variance.

Scope — committed requirements, accepted deliverables and approved changes.

Quality — defect trends, test results, rework and acceptance.

Risk — exposure, trend, mitigation progress and emerging risks.

Resources — capacity, critical skills, allocation and constraints.

Dependencies — status and impact of critical internal and external dependencies.

Predictability — consistency between commitments, forecasts, and actual delivery.
Agile and flow metrics
Throughput, cycle time, work in progress, defect trends, release frequency, product adoption, and 
customer feedback can provide useful evidence in adaptive delivery. Velocity is primarily a planning 
measure and should not be treated as a universal value or productivity metric.
Earned Value Management
EVM integrates scope, schedule, and cost through measures such as planned value, earned value, and 
actual cost. It can provide useful early warning in plan-driven initiatives with meaningful baselines. 
Agile and product environments generally require complementary flow, product, and outcome 
measures.
91

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 92
text:
Leading and lagging indicators
Lagging indicators confirm results, such as accepted milestones and realised benefits. Leading 
indicators help predict results, such as backlog health, risk trends, stakeholder engagement, resource 
capacity, and dependency health.

F5.16 — Project Closure, Transition & Benefits Realisation
Figure — Delivery-to-value lifecycle
Delivery does not end at technical completion. It ends when the enterprise has accepted the capability, 
can operate it sustainably, and can demonstrate whether the intended benefits are being realised.
Project closure
Closure includes acceptance, release of resources, contract closure, documentation, financial 
reconciliation, lessons learned, and formal confirmation that delivery responsibilities are complete.
Handover and operational readiness
Handover transfers responsibility to the operational organisation. Readiness requires appropriate 
processes, roles, skills, documentation, monitoring, support, training, and escalation arrangements.
Knowledge transfer
Operational teams must understand what was built, how it works, how it is supported, and how to 
respond to failures. Documentation supports knowledge transfer but does not replace practical 
interaction and verification.
Support transition
The support model should identify incident, request, problem, change, monitoring, escalation, 
ownership, and supplier responsibilities before operational handover.
Lessons learned
Lessons should capture what worked, what did not, why, and what should change in future delivery. 
Organisational learning requires that lessons are shared and applied.
92

title: Delivery, Projects & Programmes — page 94
text:
Benefits tracking
Benefits should be measured against baselines and targets after sufficient time has passed for outcomes 
to emerge. Variances should lead to investigation and corrective action.
Business ownership
The business should own the sustained outcome and benefits. Technology ownership of a system does 
not automatically equal ownership of the business result.
Sustainability and continuous improvement
The delivered capability must be maintained, adapted, secured, improved, and eventually retired as 
business needs evolve.

→

F5 owns the delivery journey through build, transition, and benefits realisation. F6 takes the primary 
focus from transition into operation, service support, stability, and continuous improvement.
F5.17 — Executive Delivery Case Study
An organisation has approved a major enterprise transformation involving ERP modernisation, cloud 
migration, application integration, cybersecurity improvements, data modernisation, and AI-enabled 
services. The roadmap is approved, but delivery faces competing priorities, limited resources, vendor 
dependencies, scope pressure, and executive expectations.
Executive challenge
Work through the case using the following questions:

What should be delivered, and how should the initiative be structured across projects, programmes, 
and portfolio?

Which delivery approaches are appropriate for the different components, and why?

What are the critical scope, financial, resource, risk, and dependency constraints?

How should vendors, contracts, stakeholders, and decision rights be governed?

How will quality, assurance, readiness, and delivery health be demonstrated?

Which executive metrics and management information are required?

How will transition, operational readiness, and benefits realisation be confirmed?

What should leadership decide now, and what evidence supports the recommendation?
The case is not a methodology examination. The objective is to practice executive reasoning: 
understanding trade-offs, challenging assumptions, making decisions, and maintaining the connection 
between delivery and value.
