title: Operations & Service Management — page 97
text:
F6 — Operations & Service Management
Foundation
Purpose
Build your ability to understand how enterprise technology is operated, supported, monitored, 
controlled, and continuously improved after delivery — ensuring that technology services remain 
reliable, available, secure, resilient, cost-effective, and aligned with business needs.
Delivery creates capability. Operations sustains it. By the end of this chapter, you should be able to 
answer:
"How do we run technology as reliable business services — maintaining performance, availability, 
resilience, support, and continuous improvement?"
F6.1 — What Are IT Operations & Service Management?
The business does not consume servers, networks, applications, or databases. It consumes 
services enabled by them.
This distinction is the foundation of everything in F6. Most technology organisations think in 
components: we manage servers, we patch databases, we monitor networks, we upgrade applications. 
But the business thinks in outcomes: can I process orders, can I serve customers, can I close the books, 
can I make decisions? The gap between component thinking and service thinking is where operations 
either create value or destroy it.
What IT operations means is the daily, continuous discipline of keeping technology running: monitoring 
systems, responding to events, executing procedures, managing capacity, maintaining performance, and 
ensuring availability. Operations is rarely visible when it works well, and its innovations are often 
invisible — embedded in automation, resilience, and quiet reliability. Individual operational initiatives 
may end; the discipline of operations does not.
What IT Service Management (ITSM) means is the structured, governed approach to designing, 
delivering, managing, and improving technology services. ITSM is not merely operations. It is the 
structured management of services across their lifecycle and value chain, connecting operational 
practices, governance, customer needs, and continual improvement to business outcomes. It ensures 
that technology is managed as a service, not merely as a collection of components.
Technology-centric vs. service-centric thinking is the mindset shift. Technology-centric thinking asks: 
"Is the server up?" Service-centric thinking asks: "Can the customer place an order?" Technology-centric 
97

title: Operations & Service Management — page 98
text:
thinking measures component health. Service-centric thinking measures business outcome. Both 
matter. But service-centric thinking is what separates operations that merely function from operations 
that create value.
Products, systems, platforms, and services are related but distinct. A product is what the enterprise 
acquires or builds. A system is the integrated set of components that performs a function. A platform is 
the foundational environment that enables multiple systems. A service is the consumable outcome that 
the business experiences: reliable, measurable, and governed.
Business services vs. technical services is the critical distinction. A business service is what the user 
experiences: "email," "payroll," "customer portal," "order processing." A technical service is what 
enables the business service: "Exchange server," "database cluster," "network connectivity," "API 
gateway." The business service is what matters. The technical service is what must work. Operations 
must manage both, but prioritise the business service.
Service provider and service consumer define the relationship. The technology function is the 
provider. The business function is the consumer. This relationship requires clarity: what is provided, at 
what quality, under what conditions, with what support, and at what cost. Without clarity, the 
relationship becomes transactional, adversarial, and ultimately broken.
Utility and warranty are the two dimensions of service value. Utility is what the service does: the 
functionality it provides, the capability it enables. Warranty is how the service performs: its 
availability, capacity, security, reliability. A service with high utility but poor warranty is frustrating. A 
service with high warranty but low utility is irrelevant. Both dimensions must be managed.
Service value and business outcomes are the ultimate measures. Service value is the contribution the 
service makes to business objectives: efficiency, revenue, satisfaction, risk reduction. Business outcomes 
are the measurable results: orders processed, customers served, decisions made, risks mitigated.
Operations vs. service management is the distinction between doing and governing. Operations 
executes the daily work. Service management designs, governs, and improves how that work is done. 
Both are essential. Operations without service management drifts. Service management without 
operations is theoretical.
Operational accountability means that specific individuals are responsible for specific services: their 
availability, their performance, their incidents, their changes, their improvements. Not committees. Not 
teams. Named people.
Role of IT leadership in operations is not to monitor servers or respond to alerts. It is to ensure that 
operations are structured, governed, measured, and improved as a service discipline. It is to represent 
operational reality to the executive team. It is to ensure that operational investment is proportionate to 
business risk and value.
Why service management matters is simple: without it, technology becomes a cost center that the 
business tolerates. With it, technology becomes a service provider that the business trusts. Trust is the 
currency of operational relationships.
Key principle:
The business does not consume servers, networks, applications, or databases. It consumes services enabled 
by them.
98

title: Operations & Service Management — page 99
text:
Part I — Understand the Service
F6.2 — Service Value, Customers & Business Expectations
Operations must begin with understanding what the business needs, not merely what technology does.
Business requirements define what the enterprise must achieve: process orders within four hours, 
serve customers with 99.9% availability, close monthly accounts within five business days, comply with 
regulatory reporting deadlines. These are not technical specifications. They are business outcomes that 
services must enable.
Customer and user expectations are shaped by experience: speed, reliability, accessibility, 
responsiveness, clarity. Expectations are not always articulated. They are often assumed. Operations 
must discover, document, and manage them.
Service value is the contribution the service makes to business objectives. A service that processes 
orders efficiently creates revenue value. A service that protects data creates risk value. A service that 
enables remote work creates flexibility value. Value must be understood, measured, and 
communicated.
Service experience is the sum of every interaction a user has with the service: how it performs, how it 
fails, how it is restored, how it is communicated about, how it is improved. Experience is not merely 
availability. It is the emotional and practical reality of using the service.
Business criticality ranks services by their importance to enterprise operations: revenue-generating, 
regulatory-mandated, safety-critical, supporting, discretionary. Criticality determines investment, 
priority, resilience, and response.
Service priorities define which services receive attention first when capacity is constrained, incidents 
occur, or changes conflict. Priorities must be agreed with business stakeholders, not imposed by 
technology.
Service quality is the degree to which the service meets requirements and expectations: performance, 
reliability, usability, security, support responsiveness. Quality is not a technical metric. It is a business 
judgment.
Utility and warranty reappear here as operational dimensions. Utility is what the service does. 
Warranty is how well it does it. Operations must manage both.
Service outcomes are the measurable results: orders processed, customers served, reports generated, 
decisions supported. Outcomes confirm that the service is creating value.
Business impact is the consequence of service failure: revenue lost, customers dissatisfied, regulatory 
breach, safety compromised, reputation damaged. Impact determines priority, investment, and 
resilience.
Customer satisfaction measures whether users believe the service meets their needs. It is subjective 
but essential. Dissatisfied users find workarounds, bypass controls, or abandon services.
Service ownership is the accountability for a service's performance, improvement, and value. The 
service owner is typically a business leader who understands the service's importance and can advocate 
for its needs.
99

title: Operations & Service Management — page 100
text:
Business relationship is the ongoing dialogue between service provider and consumer: expectations, 
feedback, issues, improvements, investments. It is not a contract. It is a partnership.
Service expectations vs. technical performance is the gap that operations must bridge. Technical 
performance measures component health. Service expectations measure business satisfaction. A 
technically healthy system with dissatisfied users has an operations problem. A technically degraded 
system with satisfied users may have resilient design or tolerant users — but it still has a problem.
Important distinction:
A technically healthy system does not automatically mean a satisfied customer.
F6.3 — Service Portfolio, Catalogue & Service Ownership
Services cannot be managed if they are not known. Visibility is the prerequisite of governance.
Service portfolio is the complete set of services the technology function provides or plans to provide: 
live services, services in development, services being retired. It is the strategic view of service 
investment and capability.
Service catalogue is the operational view: the live services that users can request, access, and consume. 
It is the menu of what is available, with descriptions, terms, and access mechanisms.
Business services are what users experience and consume. Technical/supporting services are what 
enable business services to function. Both must be catalogued, owned, and governed.
Service mapping traces the relationships between services: which business services depend on which 
technical services, which technical services depend on which infrastructure, which infrastructure 
depends on which suppliers. Mapping reveals fragility, concentration, and interdependency.
Service dependencies are the relationships where one service cannot function without another. A 
customer portal depends on authentication, which depends on directory services, which depend on 
network connectivity, which depends on internet access. Dependencies determine impact, priority, and 
resilience design.
Service owners are accountable for the end-to-end performance, value, and continual improvement of 
a service. Depending on the operating model, they may sit within technology or the business. Technical 
owners are accountable for the technology components and technical health that enable the service. 
Clear business ownership is also required for business outcomes and priorities. These roles must work 
together; no single perspective is sufficient.
Business owners are accountable for the business process, capability, or outcome supported by the 
service. They articulate business requirements, priorities, criticality, and impact, and share 
responsibility for benefits and adoption.
Service lifecycle is the journey from conception to retirement: design, transition, operation, 
improvement, and decommission. Each phase has distinct disciplines, risks, and governance 
requirements.
Service tiers / criticality classify services by importance: Tier 1 (business-critical, immediate response), 
Tier 2 (important, rapid response), Tier 3 (supporting, standard response), Tier 4 (discretionary, best 
effort). Tiers determine investment, resilience, and response protocols.
100

title: Operations & Service Management — page 101
text:
Service documentation captures what the service does, how it works, who owns it, how it is accessed, 
how it is supported, and how it is improved. Documentation must be accurate, accessible, and 
maintained.
Service catalogue management is the discipline of maintaining the catalogue: adding new services, 
updating existing services, retiring obsolete services, and ensuring accuracy.
Ownership and accountability mean that every service has a named owner, clear responsibilities, and 
defined escalation paths. Services without owners drift. Services with owners improve.
A simple model:
Business Service 
 Application 
 Platform 
 Infrastructure 
 Supplier
→
→
→
→
This connects naturally back to F3 architecture. Architecture designs the structure. Operations sustains 
it. Both must see the same service map.
Part II — Operate the Service
F6.4 — IT Operations Management
Operations is the engine room. It is not visible when it works well. It is all that is visible when it fails.
Daily operations are the routine activities that keep services running: system checks, batch processing, 
backup verification, log review, capacity monitoring, security scanning, patch management, and 
incident response. These are not glamorous. They are essential.
Infrastructure operations manage the physical and virtual foundation: servers, storage, networks, 
data centers, cloud resources. Infrastructure must be provisioned, monitored, maintained, and 
optimised.
Application operations manage the software systems that deliver business services: availability, 
performance, error handling, data integrity, user access, and integration health.
Cloud operations manage cloud resources: provisioning, scaling, cost optimisation, security 
configuration, compliance monitoring, and vendor management. Cloud is not hands-off. It is differently 
hands-on.
Database operations manage data repositories: performance, integrity, backup, recovery, replication, 
and optimisation. Data is a critical enterprise asset. Database operations help protect its availability, 
integrity, recoverability, and performance.
Network operations manage connectivity: internal networks, internet access, remote access, VPNs, 
wireless, and telecommunications. Networks are the nervous system of the enterprise.
Platform operations manage the foundational environments: operating systems, middleware, 
container platforms, integration platforms, and development environments.
Batch processing and scheduled jobs are the automated tasks that run at defined times: data loads, 
report generation, reconciliation, backup, and maintenance. They must be monitored, verified, and 
recovered when they fail.
Backup operations ensure that data and systems can be restored after failure. Backup is not a 
checkbox. It is a discipline: what to back up, how often, where to store, how to test, how to recover, and 
how long to retain.
101

title: Operations & Service Management — page 102
text:
Monitoring is the continuous observation of system health: performance metrics, error rates, resource 
utilisation, security events, and user activity. Monitoring detects problems before they become 
incidents.
Event handling is the response to monitoring alerts: classification, prioritisation, routing, and 
resolution. Not every event is an incident, and incidents may also be reported directly by users or other 
sources. Event management helps identify conditions that may require operational action.
Operational procedures define how routine work is performed: who does what, in what order, with 
what tools, under what conditions, and with what verification. Procedures reduce variation, increase 
reliability, and enable delegation.
Runbooks are the step-by-step guides for responding to specific situations: system failure, security 
incident, capacity exhaustion, vendor outage. They are the operational memory that prevents panic and 
enables consistent response.
Standard operating procedures (SOPs) define routine activities: provisioning, patching, backup, 
recovery, access management. They ensure consistency, compliance, and quality.
Shift operations ensure continuous coverage: who is responsible during business hours, after hours, 
weekends, holidays. Coverage gaps create vulnerability.
Operations center / NOC (Network Operations Center) is the centralised facility or function that 
monitors, coordinates, and responds to operational events. It is the nerve center of operations.
Operational handover transfers responsibility between shifts, teams, or locations: what happened, 
what is happening, what needs attention, what is scheduled. Poor handover creates gaps, duplication, 
and error.
Automation in operations reduces manual effort, increases consistency, accelerates response, and 
frees people for higher-value work. But automation also amplifies: automated errors propagate faster, 
and automated failures require human judgment to diagnose.
Executive question:
"What must happen every day for our technology services to remain healthy?"
The leader who cannot answer this question does not understand operations. The leader who can 
answer it can govern operations effectively.
F6.5 — Monitoring, Events & Observability
Modern operations depends on visibility. You cannot manage what you cannot see.
Monitoring is the continuous observation of system state: performance metrics, error rates, resource 
utilisation, security events, user activity. Monitoring tells you that something is happening.
Event management is the process of detecting, classifying, and responding to operational events: 
informational, warning, exception, and critical. Not every event requires action. But every event must 
be understood.
Alerts are the notifications that something requires attention: threshold exceeded, error detected, 
anomaly identified, failure occurred. Alerts must be actionable, accurate, and proportionate. Alert 
fatigue — too many alerts, too few meaningful — destroys operational effectiveness.
102

title: Operations & Service Management — page 103
text:
Logs are the records of system activity: what happened, when, where, who, and how. Logs are the 
forensic evidence of operations. They enable diagnosis, accountability, and compliance.
Metrics are the quantitative measures of system behaviour: response time, throughput, error rate, 
resource utilisation, availability percentage. Metrics enable trend analysis, capacity planning, and 
performance optimisation.
Traces follow a single transaction through multiple systems: where it went, how long it took, what 
failed, what succeeded. Traces reveal the path of user experience through complex architectures.
Observability is the ability to understand system behaviour from its outputs: metrics, logs, traces, and 
events. Observability is not merely monitoring. Monitoring tells you that something is wrong. 
Observability helps you understand why.
Thresholds define the boundaries of acceptable performance: response time under 2 seconds, CPU 
utilisation below 80%, error rate below 0.1%. Thresholds trigger alerts and guide intervention.
Baselines establish normal behaviour: typical performance, usual traffic patterns, standard resource 
consumption. Baselines enable anomaly detection: what is different, and why?
Health checks are the automated tests that confirm system readiness: can the service respond, is the 
database accessible, is the integration functioning, is the certificate valid?
Infrastructure monitoring observes the foundation: servers, storage, networks, data centers, cloud 
resources.
Application performance monitoring (APM) observes software behaviour: response times, error 
rates, transaction paths, user sessions, and code-level diagnostics.
Network monitoring observes connectivity: bandwidth, latency, packet loss, topology changes, and 
security events.
Synthetic monitoring simulates user transactions to test service availability and performance from 
outside the system. It reveals what users experience, not merely what components report.
User experience monitoring observes actual user interactions: page load times, click paths, 
abandonment rates, satisfaction signals. It connects technical performance to business experience.
Alert fatigue occurs when operators receive too many alerts, too few of which are actionable. It leads 
to ignored alerts, delayed response, and missed incidents. Alert management — correlation, 
prioritisation, suppression, and refinement — is essential operational discipline.
Correlation connects related events into coherent incidents: multiple alerts from the same root cause, 
cascading failures, and common-mode problems. Correlation reduces noise and accelerates diagnosis.
Anomaly detection identifies behaviour that deviates from baseline: unusual traffic, unexpected 
errors, abnormal resource consumption. Anomaly detection can reveal emerging problems before they 
trigger thresholds.
AI-assisted operations / AIOps uses machine learning to analyse operational data: predict failures, 
correlate events, recommend actions, and automate responses. AIOps amplifies human capability but 
requires quality data, clear boundaries, and human oversight.
Operational dashboards provide real-time visibility into system health: status, trends, alerts, and key 
metrics. Dashboards must be designed for decision-making, not merely for display.
Core model:
103

title: Operations & Service Management — page 104
text:
Metrics + Logs + Traces + Events 
 Operational Insight 
 Action
→
→
Data generates insight. Insight drives action. Action restores or improves service.
Important distinction:
Monitoring tells you something is wrong. Observability helps you understand why.
Part III — Support & Restore
F6.6 — Service Desk & User Support
The service desk is the human interface between technology services and their users. It is where 
operational relationship is built or broken.
Service desk purpose is not merely to log tickets. It is to restore service, answer questions, fulfill 
requests, and represent the service provider to the consumer. It is the operational face of technology.
Single point of contact means that users know where to go for help: one number, one portal, one 
channel. Fragmented contact creates confusion, delay, and frustration.
User support is the assistance provided to users: troubleshooting, guidance, training, escalation, and 
follow-up. Support quality shapes user perception of the entire service.
Tickets are the records of user requests: incidents, service requests, questions, complaints. Tickets 
enable tracking, measurement, analysis, and improvement.
Incidents are unplanned interruptions or reductions in service quality. They require rapid response 
and restoration.
Service requests are routine asks for access, information, or standard change: password reset, 
software installation, access provision, report generation. They are not incidents but must be fulfilled 
efficiently.
Queries are questions about service functionality, availability, or use. They require accurate, timely, 
and accessible answers.
Access requests are the demands for permission to use services, data, or systems. They require 
verification, authorization, provisioning, and audit.
Support channels are the mechanisms users employ: phone, email, portal, chat, mobile app, self-
service. Channel choice must match user preference, issue complexity, and operational capacity.
L1 / L2 / L3 support are the escalation tiers:

L1 (First Line) handles routine issues, service requests, and initial triage. They restore service 
quickly or route complex issues.

L2 (Second Line) handles technical diagnosis, configuration, and resolution of more complex 
problems.

L3 (Third Line) handles deep technical investigation, vendor engagement, and architectural 
resolution.
Escalation between tiers must be efficient, not bureaucratic.
Escalation is the process of raising issues that exceed current authority, capability, or time limit. 
Effective escalation is fast, transparent, and decisive.
104

title: Operations & Service Management — page 105
text:
Knowledge management captures solutions, workarounds, procedures, and guidance in accessible, 
searchable, and maintained repositories. It enables self-service, accelerates resolution, and preserves 
organisational memory.
Self-service empowers users to resolve issues, fulfill requests, and access information without human 
intervention. It reduces cost, accelerates response, and increases satisfaction — when well-designed.
Service portals are the unified interfaces for accessing services, requesting support, tracking issues, 
and consuming information. They are the digital front door of operations.
Chatbots and AI support provide automated assistance: answering questions, routing issues, 
suggesting solutions, and fulfilling routine requests. They scale support capacity but require quality 
knowledge, clear boundaries, and human fallback.
User communication keeps users informed: service status, planned maintenance, incident updates, 
and improvement announcements. Silence breeds suspicion. Transparency builds trust.
Customer experience in support is the sum of every interaction: ease of contact, speed of response, 
quality of resolution, clarity of communication, and empathy of interaction. Experience determines 
whether users see technology as an enabler or an obstacle.
Support metrics measure effectiveness: first contact resolution, mean time to resolve, customer 
satisfaction, ticket volume, backlog, and cost per ticket. Metrics enable improvement but must be 
interpreted with judgment.
Important principle:
The service desk is not simply a ticketing function. It is the operational relationship between users and 
technology services.
F6.7 — Incident Management & Major Incidents
Incident management is one of the core operational disciplines in F6.
What is an incident? An incident is an unplanned interruption to or reduction in the quality of a 
service. It is not a problem. It is not a change. It is a disruption that requires response.
Incident vs. service request is the operational distinction. An incident is something broken. A service 
request is something wanted. Confusing the two creates delay, misrouting, and frustration.
Detection is the first awareness of incident: monitoring alert, user report, automated detection, or 
operational observation. Rapid detection reduces impact.
Logging records the incident: what happened, when, where, who detected it, what was affected. 
Logging enables tracking, analysis, and accountability.
Categorization classifies the incident: type, service affected, severity, and area. Categorization enables 
routing, prioritisation, and trend analysis.
Prioritisation determines response order based on impact and urgency: how many users affected, how 
critical the service, how severe the degradation, how rapidly it is spreading.
Diagnosis identifies what is failing, what is affected, and the most effective route to restoration. It may 
identify an immediate technical cause or workaround, but exhaustive root-cause analysis belongs to 
problem management.
105

title: Operations & Service Management — page 106
text:
Escalation raises the incident to higher authority, deeper expertise, or broader coordination when it 
exceeds current capacity or time limit.
Resolution fixes the immediate cause: restart, failover, workaround, patch, configuration change. 
Resolution restores service.
Recovery confirms that service is fully restored: performance verified, functionality tested, users 
notified, monitoring active.
Closure formally completes the incident: documentation complete, root cause noted if known, follow-
up assigned if needed, and user confirmation obtained.
Priority vs. severity separates the order and urgency of response from the technical seriousness of the 
condition. Priority is typically driven by business impact and urgency; severity can describe the 
technical or operational seriousness. Organisations should define these terms consistently rather than 
assume they are interchangeable.
Impact and urgency define priority: impact is the extent of business effect; urgency is the speed of 
business requirement. Both must be assessed honestly.
SLA implications mean that incident response and resolution are governed by service level 
agreements: target response times, target resolution times, and escalation triggers. Breach has 
consequences.
Major Incident Management is the discipline for incidents that cause significant business disruption: 
dedicated leadership, coordinated response, rapid communication, and executive visibility. Major 
incidents are not merely large incidents. They are incidents that threaten enterprise operations, 
reputation, or compliance.
Major Incident Manager is the designated leader who coordinates response, communicates status, 
manages stakeholders, and ensures restoration. This role requires authority, experience, and calm 
under pressure.
War room / command structure brings together the technical, business, and communication resources 
needed for rapid, coordinated response. It is not a physical room. It is a communication and decision 
structure.
Communication during major incidents is critical: status to users, updates to executives, coordination 
with vendors, and briefing of regulators. Communication must be frequent, honest, and actionable.
Technical escalation engages deeper expertise: vendor support, specialist engineers, architecture 
review. Technical escalation must be fast and effective.
Management escalation engages senior leadership when impact exceeds thresholds, resolution 
exceeds timelines, or resources are insufficient. Management escalation must be decisive.
Vendor escalation engages suppliers when their products or services are implicated. Vendor 
relationships must include clear escalation paths.
Post-incident review examines what happened, how it was handled, what worked, what failed, and 
what should improve. It is not blame. It is learning.
Core flow:
Detect 
 Log 
 Assess 
 Restore 
 Communicate 
 Close 
 Learn
→
→
→
→
→
→
106

title: Operations & Service Management — page 107
text:
Detection begins the process. Assessment determines response. Restoration is the immediate goal. 
Communication maintains trust. Closure completes the record. Learning prevents recurrence.
Executive principle:
The first objective of incident management is to restore service — not to determine root cause.
Root cause analysis belongs to problem management. Incident management is about speed of 
restoration. Confusing the two delays recovery and prolongs impact.
F6.8 — Problem Management & Root Cause Analysis
Incidents disrupt. Problems persist. Problem management is the discipline of preventing recurrence.
Problem vs. incident is the fundamental distinction. An incident is a single disruption that requires 
immediate response. A problem is the underlying cause of one or more incidents. Incident 
management restores service. Problem management prevents recurrence.
Reactive problem management responds to incidents that have already occurred: analysing patterns, 
identifying root causes, implementing fixes, and updating knowledge. It is triggered by operational pain.
Proactive problem management anticipates problems before they cause incidents: trend analysis, 
capacity forecasting, vulnerability assessment, and preventive maintenance. It is triggered by 
operational insight.
Root cause is the fundamental reason why incidents occur: not the symptom, not the trigger, but the 
underlying condition that makes failure possible. Root cause analysis requires discipline, time, and 
honesty.
Known errors are problems with documented root causes and identified workarounds. They are not 
yet permanently fixed, but their impact can be managed.
Workarounds are temporary measures that reduce or bypass the impact of known errors: manual 
steps, alternative procedures, or temporary configurations. Workarounds enable service continuity 
while permanent fixes are developed.
Known Error Database records problems, root causes, workarounds, and resolution status. It is the 
organisational memory that accelerates incident response and guides improvement.
Trend analysis examines incident patterns: recurring issues, growing categories, seasonal variations, 
and emerging risks. Trends reveal problems before they become crises.
Recurring incidents are the signal of underlying problems. A single incident is an event. Three similar 
incidents are a pattern. Ten are a problem demanding investigation.
Root Cause Analysis (RCA) is the structured investigation of why incidents occur. It requires evidence, 
expertise, time, and independence from operational pressure.
5 Whys is the simple technique of asking "why" repeatedly until the fundamental cause is reached. It is 
not always five. It is as many as needed.
Fishbone / Ishikawa diagrams organize potential causes by category: people, process, technology, 
environment, materials, and management. They ensure comprehensive investigation.
Pareto analysis identifies the vital few causes that produce the majority of incidents: 80% of incidents 
from 20% of problems. It focuses improvement where impact is greatest.
107

title: Operations & Service Management — page 108
text:
Corrective actions fix the root cause: design change, process revision, training update, or configuration 
correction. They prevent recurrence.
Preventive actions address conditions that could cause future problems: capacity increase, monitoring 
enhancement, procedure update, or risk mitigation.
Problem ownership is the accountability for investigating, resolving, and preventing problems. The 
problem owner ensures that root cause analysis is completed, corrective actions are implemented, and 
effectiveness is verified.
Problem reviews assess whether problem management is effective: trends, backlogs, resolution rates, 
recurrence rates, and improvement impact.
Knowledge capture ensures that problem insights are documented, shared, and applied: known errors, 
workarounds, preventive measures, and lessons learned.
Core distinction:
Incident Management restores the service. Problem Management prevents recurrence.
Part IV — Control Change & Reliability
F6.9 — Change Enablement & Operational Change Control
Change is the leading cause of service disruption. Managing change is the discipline of enabling 
improvement while protecting stability.
This section requires careful boundary definition. F4 covers organisational and transformation change. 
F5 covers project scope and change control. F6 covers operational and service change.
Operational change is the modification of live services: configuration updates, patch deployment, 
capacity adjustments, access changes, and routine maintenance. It is not project delivery. It is the 
continuous evolution of operational services.
Change enablement is the governed process for authorizing, scheduling, and implementing 
operational changes. It is not change prevention. It is change discipline.
Standard change is low-risk, well-understood, and pre-authorised: routine maintenance, predefined 
updates, automated deployments. Standard changes proceed with minimal review but maximum 
automation and monitoring.
Normal change requires assessment and authorization: risk evaluation, impact analysis, testing 
verification, and approval by appropriate authority. Most operational changes are normal.
Emergency change is required to resolve or prevent major incidents: rapid authorization, abbreviated 
testing, heightened monitoring, and post-implementation review. Emergency changes are necessary but 
risky. They must be rare, fast, and carefully governed.
Change request documents the proposed change: what, why, when, how, who, risk, impact, testing, 
backout, and communication. It is the basis for assessment and authorization.
Risk assessment evaluates the probability and impact of change failure: service disruption, data loss, 
security exposure, compliance breach, and operational confusion.
Impact assessment identifies affected services, users, systems, dependencies, and operations. Impact 
determines scheduling, communication, and preparation.
108

title: Operations & Service Management — page 109
text:
Change authority is the person or body authorised to approve a change at the appropriate level. 
Standard changes may be pre-authorised; normal changes should use a proportionate authority based 
on risk and impact; emergency changes use an expedited designated authority or ECAB where 
appropriate.
CAB (Change Advisory Board) advises on and, where the organisation assigns it authority, may 
authorize higher-risk or higher-impact changes. Not every normal change should require CAB review; 
approval should be proportionate to risk, impact, and organisational policy.
Emergency CAB / ECAB supports expedited assessment and authorization of emergency changes where 
the operating model uses such a body: designated participants, rapid review, proportionate testing, and 
heightened monitoring.
Change calendar shows scheduled changes: what is changing, when, and what conflicts exist. It 
prevents collision, enables coordination, and supports communication.
Change conflicts occur when multiple changes affect the same service, system, or time window. 
Conflict management requires visibility, coordination, and sometimes deferral.
Maintenance windows are the scheduled periods when changes are permitted: low-traffic times, 
planned downtime, or designated change slots. They balance change need with service protection.
Implementation plan defines how the change will be executed: steps, sequence, verification, 
monitoring, and rollback triggers.
Testing confirms that the change works as intended: functional testing, integration testing, 
performance testing, and user acceptance. Testing must be proportionate to risk.
Backout / rollback plan defines how to reverse or otherwise recover from a change if it fails: triggers, 
procedures, verification, and communication. Every material change should have an appropriate 
recovery approach; for some changes, rollback may not be technically possible and an alternative 
remediation plan is required.
Change communication informs affected users, support teams, and stakeholders: what is changing, 
when, why, and what to expect. Silence creates surprise. Surprise creates incidents.
Post-implementation review assesses whether the change achieved its intent, whether it caused 
unintended effects, and what should be improved. It is the learning loop of change management.
Failed changes are changes that did not achieve their intent or caused unintended harm. They require 
investigation, remediation, and process improvement.
Change success rate measures the proportion of changes that achieve their intent without causing 
incidents. It is a key operational health indicator.
Boundary:
Chapter
Change Focus
F4
Organisational / transformation change
F5
Project scope / change control
F6
Operational / service change enablement
109

title: Operations & Service Management — page 110
text:
This distinction is very important for North Star. Confusing these boundaries creates governance gaps, 
overlaps, and failures.
F6.10 — Release, Deployment & Configuration Management
Changes must move safely from development through testing into production. This movement requires 
discipline, visibility, and control.
Release management plans, schedules, and controls the movement of changes into live operation. It 
ensures that releases are coherent, tested, and ready.
Deployment management executes the technical movement: packaging, installation, configuration, 
verification, and monitoring. It ensures that what was tested is what is deployed.
Release planning defines what will be released, when, to whom, and with what preparation. It 
coordinates multiple changes into coherent release packages.
Deployment strategies define how changes are introduced:

Big bang — all at once, high risk, high coordination

Phased — gradually, by segment, by region, by user group

Canary — to a small subset first, monitoring, then expanding

Blue-green — parallel environments, switching traffic, instant rollback

Rolling — incremental replacement, continuous operation
The right strategy depends on risk, scale, architecture, and capability.
Production environments are where live services run. Access is restricted, changes are controlled, and 
monitoring is intense. Production is not a test environment.
Development / Test / UAT / Production are the progression environments: development for creation, 
test for verification, UAT for user validation, production for live operation. Each environment must 
mirror production sufficiently to ensure confidence.
Release windows are the scheduled periods when deployment is permitted. They balance change 
velocity with service protection.
Rollback is the reversal of deployment when failure is detected. Rollback must be planned, tested, and 
executable within defined time limits.
Version control tracks what code, configuration, and documentation exists in which environment. It 
ensures that changes are traceable, reproducible, and auditable.
Configuration management is the discipline of identifying, controlling, and maintaining configuration 
items: hardware, software, networks, documentation, and relationships.
Configuration Items (CIs) are the components that must be managed: servers, applications, databases, 
network devices, licenses, and documents. Each CI has attributes, relationships, and lifecycle state.
CMDB (Configuration Management Database) is a repository used to record configuration items, 
relevant attributes, and relationships. In modern environments, configuration knowledge may be 
federated across discovery, cloud, asset, and platform sources; the objective is trusted configuration 
information, not a database for its own sake.
110

title: Operations & Service Management — page 111
text:
Service configuration is the complete set of CIs and relationships that deliver a service. Understanding 
service configuration enables impact analysis, change assessment, and incident diagnosis.
Asset vs. configuration item is the distinction between financial tracking and operational 
management. An asset is tracked for accounting: cost, depreciation, ownership. A CI is managed for 
operations: function, relationship, state, and change. The same component may be both.
Dependency mapping traces how CIs connect: which application depends on which database, which 
database depends on which storage, which storage depends on which network. Dependencies 
determine impact and guide response.
Configuration baselines are the approved, verified states of configuration at defined points. They 
provide reference points for comparison, rollback, and audit.
Discovery is the automated identification of CIs and their relationships. It ensures CMDB accuracy 
without manual maintenance.
Configuration accuracy is the degree to which the CMDB reflects reality. Inaccurate configuration data 
undermines change management, incident response, and impact analysis.
Important relationship:
Service 
 Components 
 Configuration Items 
 Dependencies
→
→
→
Architecture designs this structure. Operations maintains it. Both must see the same map.
F6.11 — Availability, Capacity & Performance Management
Reliability is not an accident. It is the result of deliberate design, continuous monitoring, and proactive 
management.
Availability is the proportion of time that a service is operational and accessible. It is measured as a 
percentage: 99%, 99.9%, 99.99%, 99.999%. Each additional “nine” sharply reduces the allowable 
downtime and typically demands greater engineering, operational discipline, and investment.
Uptime is the operational time. Downtime is the interruption time. Both must be measured honestly, 
including planned maintenance, unplanned failures, and partial degradation.
Planned vs. unplanned outage is the distinction between scheduled maintenance and unexpected 
failure. Both affect availability but require different governance, communication, and measurement.
Service availability is the business-facing measure: can users access the service, perform transactions, 
and complete tasks? It is not merely component uptime.
High availability is the architectural and operational design that minimizes downtime: redundancy, 
failover, load balancing, and rapid recovery. High availability is not free. It requires investment, 
complexity, and continuous attention.
Redundancy provides backup components that assume function when primary components fail: 
duplicate servers, mirrored databases, alternate networks. Redundancy increases reliability but also 
complexity and cost.
Single points of failure are components whose failure would interrupt service. Identifying and 
eliminating single points of failure is essential reliability engineering.
111

title: Operations & Service Management — page 112
text:
Capacity is the maximum workload a service can handle: transactions per second, concurrent users, 
data volume, processing throughput. Capacity must be sufficient for current demand and adaptable for 
future growth.
Demand is the actual workload: current, forecast, peak, and trend. Understanding demand enables 
planning, optimisation, and investment.
Utilisation is the proportion of capacity currently consumed. High utilisation risks saturation. Low 
utilisation wastes investment. The right utilisation depends on criticality, variability, and cost.
Capacity planning forecasts future demand and ensures sufficient capacity: when to scale, when to 
invest, when to optimise. It is not merely buying more. It is understanding need, timing, and efficiency.
Scalability is the ability to increase capacity as demand grows: vertical scaling (bigger components), 
horizontal scaling (more components), or elastic scaling (automatic adjustment).
Elasticity is the automatic expansion and contraction of capacity based on real-time demand. It is the 
cloud's defining operational advantage.
Forecasting predicts future demand based on trend, seasonality, growth, and planned change. 
Forecasting enables proactive investment rather than reactive crisis.
Performance is how the service responds under load: response time, latency, throughput, and resource 
efficiency. Performance determines user experience and operational cost.
Response time is the duration between request and response. It is the most visible performance metric 
to users.
Latency is the delay in data transmission: network latency, processing latency, storage latency. Latency 
accumulates across components and determines total response time.
Throughput is the volume of work processed per unit time: transactions per minute, reports per hour, 
messages per second.
Resource utilisation measures how intensively components are used: CPU, memory, storage, network. 
High utilisation risks saturation. Low utilisation suggests inefficiency.
Bottlenecks are the components that limit overall performance: the slowest database query, the most 
congested network link, the most overloaded server. Bottleneck identification enables targeted 
optimisation.
Performance baselines establish normal behaviour under typical load. They enable anomaly detection 
and trend analysis.
Performance trends reveal gradual degradation: slowing response, growing latency, increasing errors. 
Trends enable proactive intervention before failure.
Executive question:
"Do we have enough capacity, availability, and performance to meet current and future business 
demand?"
The leader who cannot answer this question is gambling with operational reliability.
112

title: Operations & Service Management — page 113
text:
Part V — Govern Service Performance
F6.12 — Service Levels, SLAs, OLAs & Supplier Performance
Service level management is the discipline of defining, negotiating, monitoring, and improving the 
quality of services. It is where operational commitment meets business expectation.
Service Level Management is the practice of ensuring that services meet agreed standards and 
continuously improve. It is not merely measurement. It is relationship management.
SLA (Service Level Agreement) is a documented agreement between a service provider and customer 
that defines agreed service levels, responsibilities, measurement, and relevant conditions. Commercial 
remedies and pricing may sit in an associated contract. An SLA is not simply a number; it expresses 
agreed service expectations and outcomes.
SLO (Service Level Objective) is a specific measurable target for a service level indicator. SLOs may 
support an SLA or be used internally to manage reliability and performance; they are often set with 
sufficient operating margin to protect external commitments.
OLA (Operational Level Agreement) is the internal agreement between provider teams: what one 
team commits to another to enable end-to-end service delivery. OLAs ensure that internal coordination 
supports external commitment.
Underpinning contracts are the agreements with suppliers that support service delivery: vendor SLAs, 
support contracts, and maintenance agreements. They must align with and support enterprise SLAs.
Service targets define specific, measurable standards: availability percentage, response time, 
resolution time, throughput, error rate. Targets must be achievable, meaningful, and monitored.
Availability targets specify the required uptime: 99.5%, 99.9%, 99.99%. Higher targets require greater 
investment, redundancy, and operational discipline.
Response targets specify how quickly the service desk or support team must acknowledge and begin 
working on an incident or request.
Resolution targets specify how quickly issues must be fixed: initial response, temporary workaround, 
permanent resolution.
Performance targets specify acceptable service behaviour: response time, throughput, latency, and 
resource consumption.
Service credits may be defined contractually as financial remedies for certain SLA breaches. They are 
not inherent to every SLA and should complement, not replace, operational correction and supplier 
improvement.
Supplier SLAs extend service level management to vendors: their availability, support responsiveness, 
resolution commitment, and quality standards. Supplier performance must be monitored, reviewed, 
and governed.
SLA measurement tracks actual performance against targets: availability, response time, resolution 
time, and customer satisfaction. Measurement must be honest, consistent, and transparent.
SLA breaches occur when performance falls below target. Breach management requires investigation, 
communication, remedy, and improvement. Repeated breaches require escalation and contractual 
action.
113

title: Operations & Service Management — page 114
text:
Reporting communicates SLA performance to stakeholders: trends, breaches, improvements, and 
investments. Reporting must be clear, actionable, and honest.
Service reviews are the periodic meetings between provider and consumer to discuss performance, 
issues, improvements, and changes. They are the operational relationship in action.
Experience Level Agreements (XLAs) extend beyond traditional SLAs to measure user experience: 
satisfaction, effort, sentiment, and outcome. XLAs recognise that technical performance does not 
guarantee user satisfaction.
Important model:
Business Expectation 
 SLA 
 OLA 
 Supplier Commitment 
 Service Performance
→
→
→
→
Business expectations drive SLA targets. SLAs drive OLA requirements. OLAs drive supplier 
commitments. Supplier commitments enable service performance. Misalignment at any point breaks 
the chain.
And:
An SLA is not simply a number. It is an agreement about expected service outcomes.
F6.13 — Suppliers, Managed Services & Operational Partners
No enterprise operates technology alone. Suppliers, providers, and partners are integral to service 
delivery. Governing them is integral to operations.
Managed service providers deliver operational services on behalf of the enterprise: infrastructure 
management, application support, security operations, or service desk. They extend enterprise 
capability but do not replace enterprise accountability.
Outsourcing transfers specific functions to external providers: development, operations, support, or 
infrastructure. Outsourcing reduces direct control but can improve scale, expertise, and cost efficiency. 
Accountability remains with the enterprise.
Cloud providers deliver infrastructure, platform, and software services. Their operational 
performance directly affects enterprise service quality. Cloud governance is operational governance.
SaaS providers deliver application services. Their availability, performance, and security are 
enterprise concerns. SaaS management requires vendor oversight, integration governance, and data 
protection.
Support contracts define the operational relationship with vendors: response times, resolution 
commitments, escalation paths, and service credits. They must be monitored and enforced.
Supplier governance ensures that external providers deliver as committed: performance review, 
contract compliance, risk monitoring, and relationship management. Governance is not adversarial. It 
is the discipline of ensuring partnership delivers value.
Operational Level Agreements define internal commitments between teams that support end-to-end 
service delivery. They must align with and support external SLAs.
Underpinning contracts are the agreements with suppliers that enable service delivery. They must be 
visible, aligned, and governed.
114

title: Operations & Service Management — page 115
text:
Vendor escalation is the mechanism for addressing supplier underperformance: operational 
escalation, commercial escalation, and contractual action. Escalation paths must be defined before they 
are needed.
Supplier performance must be measured continuously: availability, responsiveness, quality, and 
value. Performance data enables objective conversation and informed decisions.
Multi-vendor environments require coordination: multiple suppliers delivering interdependent 
services. Without coordination, gaps emerge, conflicts occur, and accountability fragments.
Service Integration and Management (SIAM) is the discipline of integrating multiple suppliers into a 
coherent service delivery ecosystem. SIAM provides governance, coordination, and end-to-end 
accountability across vendor boundaries.
Shared service outcomes require coordinated responsibilities across enterprise teams and suppliers. 
Contracts and operating models should make responsibilities explicit, while end-to-end accountability 
for the service remains clear within the enterprise.
End-to-end service ownership means that someone in the enterprise is accountable for service quality 
regardless of how many suppliers contribute. Ownership cannot be outsourced.
Vendor dependency is the risk that the enterprise relies too heavily on a single supplier for critical 
capability. Dependency reduces leverage, increases cost, and constrains flexibility.
Service reviews are the periodic assessments of supplier performance: what worked, what failed, what 
improved, what needs attention. Reviews must be honest, documented, and action-oriented.
Supplier improvement plans address persistent underperformance: specific deficiencies, 
improvement targets, timelines, resources, and verification. Plans must be tracked and enforced.
At Foundation level, SIAM belongs here because F5 addresses commercial delivery and vendor 
selection, while F6 addresses ongoing operational supplier performance, coordination, and end-to-end 
service integration.
F6.14 — Operational Metrics, KPIs & Service Reporting
Measurement is the discipline of knowing whether operations are healthy. Without measurement, 
operations drifts. With poor measurement, operations optimizes the wrong things.
Service availability is the proportion of time services are operational. It is the most visible operational 
metric.
SLA achievement measures whether services meet their agreed targets: availability, response time, 
resolution time, and performance. Achievement confirms commitment. Breach signals problem.
Incident volume tracks the number of disruptions: total incidents, by service, by category, by severity, 
by trend. Volume reveals stability or fragility.
Major incidents count the disruptions that caused significant business impact. Frequency of major 
incidents is a critical health indicator.
Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) measures how quickly problems are identified: from occurrence to 
awareness. Rapid detection reduces impact.
Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA) measures how quickly incidents are recognised and response 
initiated: from detection to assignment. Rapid acknowledgment accelerates recovery.
115

title: Operations & Service Management — page 116
text:
Mean Time to Restore / Recover (MTTR) measures how quickly service is restored: from detection to 
recovery. Rapid restoration minimizes business impact.
First Contact Resolution measures the proportion of issues resolved at first support interaction. It 
indicates support effectiveness and knowledge quality.
Resolution time measures how long incidents take to fix: from logging to closure. It reflects support 
capability, complexity, and process efficiency.
Reopened tickets measure incidents that were closed prematurely or incompletely: returned by users, 
recurring symptoms, or unresolved root causes. Reopened tickets signal quality failure.
Backlog measures unresolved work: incidents, problems, changes, requests. Growing backlog indicates 
capacity constraint, process failure, or demand surge.
Change success rate measures the proportion of changes that achieve their intent without causing 
incidents. It reflects change discipline and operational maturity.
Failed change rate measures changes that caused incidents or required rollback. It signals process 
weakness or risk underestimation.
Problem recurrence measures whether problems are truly fixed or merely suppressed. Recurrence 
indicates ineffective root cause analysis or incomplete corrective action.
Capacity utilisation measures how intensively resources are used: CPU, memory, storage, network. It 
enables optimisation and investment planning.
Customer satisfaction measures user perception of service quality: responsiveness, effectiveness, 
communication, and empathy. Satisfaction is subjective but essential.
Service experience extends beyond satisfaction to measure effort, emotion, and outcome: how easy 
was it, how did it feel, did it work?
Cost per service / ticket measures operational efficiency: total cost divided by volume. It enables 
comparison, benchmarking, and optimisation. But cost reduction must not degrade quality.
Trend analysis examines metrics over time: improving, degrading, stable, cyclical, or anomalous. 
Trends reveal patterns that single points miss.
Executive dashboards provide concise, visual, real-time operational health: status, trends, alerts, and 
key metrics. Dashboards must highlight what matters for decision-making.
Leading vs. lagging indicators is the measurement discipline. Lagging indicators confirm results: 
availability achieved, incidents resolved, costs incurred. Leading indicators predict results: monitoring 
coverage, change backlog, training completion, knowledge freshness. Effective measurement tracks 
both.
But emphasize:
Metrics should support decisions, not merely produce reports.
The organisation that measures everything and decides nothing is not data-driven. It is data-drowned. 
The discipline is in selecting the metrics that matter, interpreting them with judgment, and acting on 
them with speed.
116

title: Operations & Service Management — page 117
text:
Part VI — Sustain & Improve
F6.15 — Knowledge Management & Operational Documentation
A service that depends on what one person remembers is not operationally mature. Knowledge must be 
captured, shared, maintained, and applied.
Knowledge management is the discipline of creating, organizing, sharing, and maintaining the 
information that enables operations: procedures, solutions, workarounds, insights, and lessons.
Knowledge articles are the documented solutions to known issues: symptoms, causes, resolutions, and 
verification. They enable rapid incident response and self-service.
Known errors are the documented problems with identified root causes and available workarounds. 
They accelerate incident response while permanent fixes are developed.
Runbooks are the step-by-step procedures for operational tasks: system startup, failover execution, 
backup verification, incident response. They are the operational memory that enables consistent 
execution.
SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) define routine activities: provisioning, patching, access 
management, change implementation. They ensure consistency, compliance, and quality.
Technical documentation captures system design, configuration, architecture, and interfaces. It 
enables understanding, maintenance, and evolution.
Support documentation captures service information: what the service does, who uses it, how to 
access it, how to get help, and what to expect. It empowers users and reduces support burden.
Service documentation combines business and technical information: service description, owner, 
dependencies, SLAs, contacts, and procedures. It is the single source of service truth.
Knowledge ownership is the accountability for maintaining specific knowledge: accuracy, currency, 
completeness, and accessibility. Knowledge without ownership decays.
Knowledge transfer ensures that expertise moves from individuals to the organisation: 
documentation, training, mentoring, and shadowing. Transfer prevents loss when people leave.
Knowledge retention preserves organisational memory: capturing expertise before departure, 
documenting decisions, and maintaining historical context.
Shift handover transfers operational context between teams: what happened, what is happening, what 
needs attention, what is scheduled. Poor handover creates gaps and errors.
Vendor knowledge transfer ensures that external expertise becomes internal capability: training, 
documentation, shadowing, and practice. Dependency on vendor knowledge creates risk.
Self-service knowledge empowers users to resolve issues independently: searchable articles, guided 
procedures, and automated assistance. It reduces cost and accelerates resolution.
Lessons learned capture insights from incidents, changes, projects, and reviews: what worked, what 
failed, what should change. They must be documented, shared, and applied.
Knowledge quality measures accuracy, completeness, currency, accessibility, and usefulness. Poor 
knowledge is worse than no knowledge because it creates false confidence.
117

title: Operations & Service Management — page 118
text:
AI-assisted knowledge management uses machine learning to suggest solutions, auto-generate 
articles, identify gaps, and improve search. It amplifies human effort but requires quality data and clear 
governance.
Core principle:
A service that depends on what one person remembers is not operationally mature.
F6.16 — Automation, AIOps & Intelligent Operations
Operations is evolving from manual execution to intelligent adaptation. This section creates an 
important connection back to F2 without repeating AI fundamentals.
Operational automation replaces manual tasks with automated execution: provisioning, patching, 
backup, monitoring, alerting, and remediation. Automation increases speed, consistency, and scale. It 
also amplifies error and requires governance.
Workflow automation orchestrates sequences of operational tasks: incident routing, change approval, 
access provisioning, and report generation. It reduces delay and enforces process.
Infrastructure automation manages cloud and on-premises resources as code: provisioning, 
configuration, scaling, and retirement. It enables consistency, repeatability, and auditability.
Automated remediation responds to detected issues without human intervention: restart failed 
services, reroute traffic, scale resources, or apply workarounds. It accelerates recovery but requires 
careful boundary definition.
Self-healing is the advanced form of automated remediation: systems that detect, diagnose, and resolve 
issues without human involvement. Self-healing reduces operational burden but requires robust design 
and human oversight.
Event correlation connects related operational events into coherent incidents: multiple alerts from the 
same root cause, cascading failures, and common-mode problems. Correlation reduces noise and 
accelerates diagnosis.
AIOps (Artificial Intelligence for IT Operations) uses machine learning to analyse operational data: 
predict failures, correlate events, recommend actions, and automate responses. AIOps amplifies human 
capability but requires quality data, clear boundaries, and continuous validation.
Predictive operations anticipates problems before they cause incidents: capacity exhaustion, 
performance degradation, failure patterns, and anomaly detection. Prediction enables proactive 
intervention.
Anomaly detection identifies behaviour that deviates from baseline: unusual traffic, unexpected 
errors, abnormal resource consumption. Anomaly detection reveals emerging problems before 
thresholds are breached.
AI-assisted service desk uses natural language processing to understand user requests, suggest 
solutions, route issues, and fulfill routine requests. It scales support capacity but requires quality 
knowledge and human fallback.
Intelligent routing directs issues to the most appropriate resolver based on content, skill, availability, 
and history. It reduces resolution time and improves first-contact resolution.
118

title: Operations & Service Management — page 119
text:
AI knowledge assistants help users find information, answer questions, and resolve issues through 
conversational interaction. They require curated knowledge and continuous learning.
Predictive capacity management forecasts demand and optimizes resources: when to scale, when to 
invest, when to consolidate. It improves efficiency and reduces waste.
Automation risks include over-automation, brittle scripts, cascading failures, loss of human judgment, 
and governance gaps. Automation must be governed as rigorously as manual work.
Human oversight ensures that automated systems operate within defined boundaries: escalation 
triggers, exception handling, and intervention protocols. Humans must remain accountable for 
automated decisions.
Governance of operational AI defines who decides what AI can do, how its decisions are monitored, 
how errors are corrected, and how accountability is maintained.
Progression:
Manual 
 Standardized 
 Automated 
 Predictive 
 Adaptive
→
→
→
→
Manual work requires human effort for every instance. Standardized work follows defined procedures. 
Automated work executes without human intervention. Predictive work anticipates and prevents. 
Adaptive work learns and optimizes continuously.
F6.17 — Continual Improvement & Service Maturity
Figure — Service operations and continual improvement
Stable operations are not static operations. The discipline of improvement is what separates mature 
operations from declining ones.
119

title: Operations & Service Management — page 120
text:
Continual improvement is the ongoing practice of identifying opportunities, prioritizing actions, 
implementing changes, and verifying results. It is not a project. It is a permanent organisational habit.
Improvement opportunities emerge from many sources: incidents, problems, changes, audits, 
feedback, benchmarks, and innovation. They must be captured, evaluated, and prioritised.
Improvement register is the inventory of identified opportunities: description, benefit, cost, risk, 
priority, owner, and status. It ensures that opportunities are not lost and that improvement is visible.
Baselines establish current performance: availability, cost, satisfaction, efficiency, and quality. 
Baselines enable measurement of improvement.
Targets define desired future performance: specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound. 
Targets provide direction and motivation.
Prioritisation determines which improvements to pursue: impact, feasibility, resource requirement, 
strategic alignment, and risk. Not every opportunity should be pursued. The discipline is in choosing 
wisely.
Root-cause-driven improvement addresses the fundamental causes of operational pain: recurring 
incidents, chronic problems, process failures, and capability gaps. It prevents symptoms rather than 
treating them.
Automation opportunities identify where manual effort can be reduced, consistency increased, and 
speed accelerated. Automation is a primary lever of operational improvement.
Customer feedback reveals where services fail to meet expectations: complaints, suggestions, surveys, 
and behavioural data. Feedback is the voice of the user in improvement.
Service reviews assess service performance, identify improvement areas, and commit to action. They 
are the operational dialogue between provider and consumer.
Operational maturity describes the sophistication of operational practices: from ad hoc to defined, 
from defined to measured, from measured to managed, from managed to optimised. Maturity is not a 
destination. It is a continuous journey.
Process maturity describes the sophistication of specific operational processes: incident management, 
change enablement, problem management, service level management. Each process matures 
independently and requires individual attention.
Service maturity describes the overall capability of a service: its reliability, efficiency, responsiveness, 
and value. Mature services are predictable, cost-effective, and aligned to business need.
Benchmarking compares operational performance against peers, standards, or aspirational targets. 
Benchmarking reveals gaps, validates progress, and identifies opportunities.
Lessons learned capture insights from operational experience: what worked, what failed, what should 
change. They must be documented, shared, and applied.
Improvement ownership is the accountability for specific improvements: identifying, planning, 
implementing, and verifying. Improvements without owners are wishes.
Benefits measurement confirms that improvement achieved its intent: cost reduced, quality increased, 
speed accelerated, satisfaction improved. Measurement validates investment and guides future 
prioritisation.
Simple model:
120

title: Operations & Service Management — page 121
text:
Measure 
 Understand 
 Prioritise 
 Improve 
 Verify 
 Repeat
→
→
→
→
→
Measurement reveals current state. Understanding identifies causes and opportunities. Prioritisation 
focuses effort. Improvement implements change. Verification confirms results. Repetition sustains 
discipline.
Core principle:
Stable operations are not static operations.
The enterprise that believes it has achieved operational excellence and stops improving is already 
declining. Excellence is not a state. It is a practice.
F6.18 — Executive Operations Case Study
This section brings F6 together through an integrated scenario. Read it as an exercise in applying 
everything this chapter has established.
The situation:
A critical enterprise digital service is experiencing recurring outages, slow response times, growing 
ticket volumes, failed changes, vendor disputes, poor SLA performance, incomplete monitoring, and 
frustrated business users.
The learner must determine:

What is the immediate operational priority? — Which incidents, problems, or risks demand 
urgent attention?

Which incidents require major-incident handling? — What criteria trigger major incident 
response, and what structure is needed?

What recurring problems require root-cause investigation? — Which patterns indicate 
underlying problems that incident management alone cannot solve?

Is monitoring and observability sufficient? — What visibility exists, what is missing, and what 
would enable faster detection and diagnosis?

Are operational changes properly controlled? — What is the change success rate, what failures 
occurred, and what governance is needed?

Are SLAs and supplier responsibilities appropriate? — Do agreements reflect business need, are 
they monitored, and are they enforced?

Which KPIs should executives monitor? — What metrics reveal operational health, and what 
decisions do they enable?

What should be automated or improved? — Where does manual effort create risk or delay, and 
where would improvement create greatest value?
Then:

What should leadership do now, and why? — What decisions, investments, or interventions are 
required, with what rationale and what expected outcome?
The scenario uses structured questions and emphasises reasoning over prescribed answers.
